MUNICIPAL RIAICTIOFS. 1905. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE TOWN HALL WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN. -

There has never been an occasion, I beg to assure you, upon which a more solemn responsibility has rested upon the ratepayers of your ward than in the election of next week. For over four year'. along with others, I have been trying to induce the burgesses of Warrington to set their faces against the immoral and Illegal trad- ing of nymbers of the Town Council with the Corporatioa and three years ago you elected me by a magnificent majority to the Couneil Chamber. in order that I might help in stamping this out, and in the effort to lift municipal affairs out of the rut of party—ln my opinion then as now, the cause of almost all civic troubles, and the curse of municipal life. I submitted then, as I sub- mit now, that the duty of the wise citizen is to select a representative because he is competent, fearless, and honest, and not because he is blue, green or red—that is the nominee of either of the political parties. The late Mr. John Cronfleld was strongly of this opinion, as is the present head of the United States of America, Preeldent Roosevelt. for whom Mr. A. H. Crosfield expressed such unbounded admiration a few days ago. In his great fight against Tammany for the Mayoralty of New York City,and in which he was beaten, President Roosevelt used these memorable words . .

•• The worst evils that affect our local Government arise from and are the inevitable result of the mixing up of city affairs with the party politics of the nation and of the State. The lines upon which national parties divide have no necessary connection with the business of the city, such connection opens the was to countless schemes of public plunder and civic

corruption." This has been the appalling result in Warrington. The two parties fought till they began to see that by a compact they could Save themselves the heavy expenses of municipal contests, fill tha Council Chamber with docile jelly-fish dummies, and pursue their selfish aims with the deplorable results which have shocked the town and made it a byevord throughout the country. And so since four years ago, I and those associated with me have sought at great personal inconvenience and expense to persuade the ratepayers to elect men, not because they are Conseryati, e, Liberal, or Labour, but because they are trustworthy, and have backbone. The result already of our efforts has been marked. The out- lay on extravagant schemes, such for instance as the new police court, has been entirely stopped, and ridiculous proposals such as the suggested new staircase at the Technical &hoots, to cost some thousands of pounds, have been defeated. The capital expenditure undertaken in the few years prior to our intervention (including the notorious Lawson Water Contract) amounted to severs Z hundred thousands of pounds, subse- quently apart from new schoots required, it has been practically nothing; immoral and illegal trading has been broucrht to an end, and the rates, apart from the New Education Act rate, have been sensibly reduced this year, and, according to Councillor Burton, are likely to be further reduced next year. For this you have the Non-Traders and the Non-Traders solely to thank. To my profound amazement and to their lasting dis- credit, the executive of the Warrington Libor's' Assoc's- tion, as has been publicly stated, decided a few weeks ago to promote Municipal Contests on the let November proximo iR every Ward of the Town with the object, not of improving the representation, but of getting their fighting machinery into good order, in other words to prostitute the important municipal interests of the town and to treat them as mere counters in the Parliamentary game ; to convert the municipal elections into m-re tt wheel-greasers "for the Liberal party, in view of the coming general election I To the credit of the many Liberals who have been waited upon and urged by their Leaders to oppose retiring Non-Traders, such as Mr. Councillor Pemberton, they have declined to do so in view of the good work accomplished by them, and so five out of the six mem- bers of the Council already returned without opposition are either Non-Traders, or are in entire sympathy with Non-Trading. This is a well-deserved snub for the Liberal Execu- tive ; I now desire to appeal to my fellow-Liberals in the Town Hall Ward to vote for Mr. Benson and thew the Liberal Executive that as "the Kingdom of Heaven must be first pure thtn peaceable," there will be no peace for the Liberal party in Warrington until those who have used it for their own selfish ends have been turned out of it bag and baggage, and until the party is run on abso- lutely clean and moral lines. I am well aware that Mr. Benson's opponent claims to be a thorough Non-Trader, that Indeed all the six candidates for the three seats to be fought for next Wednesday make the same claim I I earnestly appeal however, to all Non-Traders, whether Conservative, Labour or Liberal in your ward, not to be misled, but to vote and to vote early for dr. Benson, the tried and approved Non-Trading candidate. In conclusion, I hope you will believe that I have no personal end in view in thus addressing you, indeed there is no public office or position in Warrington that I seek or would accept. and that my sole object is the truest and best interests of the people of your Ward and of the Town. I am, Ladles and Gentlemen, Your faithful servant, JAMBS DODDS.

mess; but, unfortunately, he's engaged." "Where's he going to ? " Aced Bina. suspiciously. "To dine with that. bounder Faze:' fancy. Anyhow, the mater has got one of her :ommittee shows on to-night, and he won't lear of her putting it off.' "I can't understand her offering to do so: that strikes me as the funny part of it. I wonder he doesn't join it. She doesn't seem to think anything 400 good for him. I tell you, Charlie, I'm very puzzled about this :ommittee and its business, and there's a decided mystery about Mr. Stuart." "Oh, Stuart," said Charlie lightly, going off at a tangent. "He's a jolly good chap, and if you only want to discuss mysteries of your own imagining with me you must put it off till to-morrow, as I can't stop." He began to make towards the door. "Wait a minute, Charlie," she called out. "I've something more important to tell you, and it's a secret ; -mum to everyone till to- morrow." "What's it," asked her brother. "Buck op, I must be off." "I'm --well oh," began Bina, nervously, "I'm going to marry Ben I " " Whew l " whistled Charlie. Then he threw his arms round her, kissing her warmly. " Good old girl," he said enthusiastically. "I do hope you'll be happy. He's a devilish good old chap, and I know he's fond of you. But when did it happen, and what do the guv'nor and mater say ? ' "Last night," said Bina, answering both questions at once. "and they won't hear of it for some unearthly reason. There were ruc- tions last night and again this morning, and its in abeyance till to-morrow. You've got to help, Charlie dear; but not a word until you know officially." "All right, I'll help, old girl, don't you fret. You leave it to me," he went on, grandilo- quently in the exuberance of his youth, "and I'll put it through all right. I'm delighted." It's a ~ good thing someone's pleased, besides myself and Ben," said Bina, hugging him affectionately and smiling at his self- :onfidence. "Well, I must bolt," exclaimed Charlie, hurrying out of the room. "I'll see you ibout it again to-morrow." And Bina was left considerably happier for ais hasty visit. Charlie might not be a very :onvincirg advocate but he was fearless and anthusiastic. and she was badly in need of backing up. That evening she was going to Lady Grizelle's, and she had wired to ask her to be alone. There, too, she was sure of help and sympathy. Above all, she herself felt proud and fearless in the revelation of her great love. Later on in the afternoon Otto gave her to understand that he was dining with lan Frazer, and, principally from a new feeling of aostility to her mother, she expressed her lislike of him frankly. "Where did you meet him ? " she asked: ind Otto had to invent an occasion on the spot. This she followed up by several other point- ed questions, which he parried with the ut- most tact and good nature. However, despite his assurances to the contrary, as soon as Bina had started for her aunt's house no further word was said as to his dining with Frazer, and he joined the duke and duchess in the drawing-room in due :ourse. "So Frazer will not be here to-night ? " he said. "No," replied his hstess, a shade of anxiety passing over het', face; "he has the Earl of Ben Nevis dining with him. We hope to find in him a new recruit." In her heart she was devoutly sorry that his name had been suggested at the last meet - ing, when she had not had the faintest inkling of Bina's and his unlucky attachment; but it was too late now to draw back, as all arrange- ments had been made. To run the risk of sus- picion would be fatal not only to their plans but to themselves. Neither the duke nor she would allow themselves to brood in their moments alone; but she felt that had she known how far things would go she would have avoided the whore affair from the outset. Each day involved them all more deeply, and she found herself suffering from nervous twinges in her mind, which to her, with her splendid mental constitution, were quite a new sensation. And now came this entangle- ment of Bina's to complicate things still further. However, she set her lips, and her teeth underneath them, determined to face the future, come what might, whether it were success or —! She could not frame the idea of the alternative into words, but she felt that now there was only one possible :ourse of action in any event. "I hope we shall," agreed Otto sincerely. " I saw him dancing with Lady Sabina last night and was struck with the capable look of the man." "We have arranged that there are to be no formalities," said the duke, who had been in one of his dreamy moods, suddenly waking up, "until we get to Hampstead House, because of the servants. The least thing might arouse suspicion." Otto nodded acquiescence, as the guests began to arrive. One by one he was presented to them, and with each one he shook hands cordially, pass- ing some light remark. His manner was perfect in its bonhomie, and it was obvious that all the guests were impressed by his bearing and appearance. Dinner followed, and Otto gave his arm to the hostess with an easy grace. Throughout the meal he talked his best, laying himself out to be cordial to all within reach, and carefully eschewing politics, and by the time it was finished he had made everyone present his friend, if not Rudolph's. Even the one customary toast of the com- mittee was omitted for once, and the gentle- men rose with the ladies in view of the busy evening ahead. The same precautions as usual were taken as to their mode of departure, and Hamp- stead House was reached in motors, arriving singly and silently. Otto was first with the duke and Ellis Gordon, who had acted as their chauffeur. His blood was tingling with excitement, and the drive through the night air had struck a vein of romance and adventure in his heart. To-night he felt he had to play for Rudolph and a crown. He took up his stand in front of the big open fireplace with the duke on his right hand, while Ellis Gordon remained at the door to introduce the guests with due form- ality. The old dining-hall was brilliantly lit, and on the black oak tables on the dais was a profusion of gold plate and white roses. There were great dishes heaped high with every variety of fruit, and decanters filled with the luke's famous port. The whole had the appearance of a gala night rather than a meet- mg for the transaction of business. In twos and threes the rest of the conspira- tors arrived and were announced with due formality by Gordon. Then in their turn they were presented by the .Duke of Hamp- stead to Otto, whose hand they kissed, the men bowing low and the ladies curtseying to their new monarch. The latter he kissed on the cheek with an air of old-fashioned gallan- try, while to each of the men he gave a cordial grip of the hand, as they passed on to the right. In the intoxication of the moment he almost forgot his imposture, scarcely remem- bering that he was acting for another who might entirely disapprove of his actions. The ceremony of presentation over, Otto led the Duchess of Hampstead to the dais and took the central chair with his hostess on his right and the Marchioness of Swanage on his left. The others ranged themselves down the table at their allotted places with the duke at the end. When all the glasses had been filled, the duke rose from his seat, his glass in his hand, and his eyes sparkling with excitement. He bowed low to Otto. "With your majesty's permission," he began, speaking clearly and eagerly, "I have a toast to give. We, sire, your humble and obedient servants, are greatly honoured lby your presence here to-night in our midst and do most devoutly bid you welcome back to your own again. Ere long it is our 110Ou and

our trust that we shall see you publicly acknowledged on every side and seated upon your rightful throne, which was so illegally usurped from your ancestors. A great wrong was done, and it is our endeavour to right that wrong by bringing back the king from across the water. For two centuriee there have been plots and rumours of plots, but they have either been mismanaged or the mere vapourings of malcontents. But we, sire, mean to do or to die in your cause, and to-night for the first time we have the honour of seeing you face to face and the oppor- tunity of assuring you of our loyalty 4 Your presence aids us to bring our plans to a head, 3.nd shows that the time has come for action, snd we intend to act. Ere long now we shall strike a blow for God and th; right, and your Majesty shall soon come to his own again— shall soon come back across the water to stay and to rule his loyal subjects. Gentle* men," concluded the duke. whdse voice ha risen in his excitement, holding up his glass above his head. " Gentlemen, the King I His Majesty King Charles 111. of Great Britain and Ireland! God bless him I"

With one movement they all rose, pushing back their heavy chairs across the oak floor with a loud, grating sound and facing Otto, who sat with glowing cheeks and bright eyes, smiling first to one and then another and bowing time after time to both sides of the table.
They all.took up the cry. 'The King! God bless him ! "
It rang loudly through the old dining-hall as they raised their glasses and drained them. . .
The,n following the 'duke's example, they dashed them on the ground, shivering them to atoms.
CHAPTER XXI.
Orro, still smiling, rose and lifted his hand ieprecatingly to prevent cheering. In an instant silence fell on the room, and even _

, . Carruthers and Atherley foiebore to smile cynically at their own excitement. Fot even they had to confess that they had been carried out of themselves for once despite their wonted imperturbability. It was cer- tainly a moment for enthusiasm, or of what avail was the plot itself? " Dear friends," said Otto speaking gently, but not without emotion, "Clear friends—for what else have I the right or the desire to call you ?—I thank you from the bottom of hpart for your enthusiastic rerention. It
THE . . .
WHITE ROSE.
By OERALD BISS.

'The whole scene had not taken more than .r.k minute or two ; and now that it was over it seemed so simple and easy, whereas before it had seemed so impossible. It is wonderful -what barrier 3 and restraints a few words will break down; and how from commonpiaces and conveßtionalitics it is but the shortest step to confidences and unrestrained intimacy. From the awkward fencing of the preceding dance all was changed in a Hash to a frank abandonment on both sides, each endeavour- ing to tplain how their love had been simul- taneous with their first introduction, each in true lover's fashion exaggerating ,a little. " And you really do love me, darling ? " ended up Ben eagerly, despite countless assurances and satisfactory repetitions. " Yes, very really," answered Bina con- tentedly, resting very near to him. " And you are quite ready to give up flirting altogether for my sake ? " pursued the newly-accepted lover, tyrannically. " Oh, Ben, I have never, never flirted," humbly protested the girl.
" Well, we won't discuss it, dearest," said the man masterfully," so long as you promise to give it up for the future." The girl laughed merrily.
"I Promise-," she saia ; and duly sealed the promise.

" ST° more lovely drives with Mr. Stuart ? " he whispered, holding her very close and looking into her eyes. " I believe yoll are jealous." she murmered. " Why not ?" he aLked, "I want yoa all to myself." " Haven't you got me, Ben dear ? " she answered very gently; and they fell to discussing the more practical side of the question.
"I've got to face the duke," said Ben, with a long face. " Well ? " rejoined Bina, whose fear of her father was tempered by long familiarity. . .
" I don't know hOw he'll take 'it," he explained, dubiously. "I'm not a parti- cularly promising path compared with Branksea and others."

The girl smiled in an amused-fashion. " I think you are very much more promis- ing! Anyhow, I have promised to marry you ; and, what's more, I mean to, whatever anyone may say. And, really," she added, thoughtfully, " I don't see that there can be any objection to you, dear. I may, of course, be prejudiced, but I think you are quite the nicest, handsomest, and most charming man in the world—and I love you I" . "Love's delightful," responded Ben, hav- ing suitably acknowledged her strongly. worded compliment; "but it's not alwayt logical. Anyhow. I'll face the music at the earliest possible moment and have it out with your father." Her next two partners had just cause to complain to being cut; and it was with very poor grace that Ben Nevis eventually aban- doned Bina till the supper-dance. Further, Bina had to parry one or two pointed ques- tions from the duchess ps to her prolonged disappearance, but this she did most demurely. Later on, as the evening was drawing to a close, chance threw the duke and Ben Nevis into each other's arms; and the latter took the bull by the horns, asking him for a few minutes' conversation on an important topic. Bina's father, looking puzzled, nevertheless readily acceded to Ben's request; but two or three minutes served to clear up his bewilderment.

He listened to the young man without comment, his manner growing more freezing as he proceeded. When Ben had finished. he spoke: "I am sorry that matters have gone so far, and that Lady Sabina has been so precipitate. Against you personally, Lord Ben Nevis, I have not a word to say; but I must tell you, on behalf of the duchess and myself, that we have other views, other hopes for our daughter." The duke's eyes grew dreamy and far- away as he spoke. Then he suddenly re- called himself and concluded more sharply: "I will speak to Lady Sabina to-morrow on the subject, and will then communicate with you again. Good-night!" The older man left him with a formal bow before Ben had time to protest; and, to his chagrin, a few moments later when he was searching for Bina he learnt that the Duchess of Hampstead and she had just left, escorted by Mr. Stuart. During the course of the following morning he received a letter from Bina, which helpe4 to some extent to allay his anxiety. "DEAREST," it ran, "I was bundled off last night by mother without a moment's warning or a chance of seeing you, and I_ was looking forward to our
saying good-night. I saw that some- thing Was wrong; and quite a little
storm burst whe-n. we gotA home—why ' I can't understand. However, I re-
fused to yield a point, except to promise
not to see-you for- a whole da'y ; and now I wish I hadn't, as it seems such a fear-
fully long time without you ! lam to think it over quietly ; but I know what
, my answer will be, and you need have no fear, my darling. lam perfectly happy How
in the ' knowledge of your .love.
I could ever have gone on so long without it, I don't know; but now I have it, I
don't mean to lose it.
Meet me in the
Park, where we met the other clay. at

noon to-morrow, and we can talk t-hings out. My promise will be up then; and I shall have seen father and mother again, on the subject. I believe they want me to marry this mysterious Mr. Stuart ! But I told them last night that if they did'nt consent gracefully I feared we should have .to get married
without; and it was an idea, that never seemed to have entered their heads. Be
sure I shall be true to you, my heart's own darling, and do not fear the result. All my love is yours till death.
Ben sighed, half with relief, half with . _ _ .
- anxiety, when he _received this .strange first

Love-letter. He had known all along that he need have no fear of Bina ; but twenty-four hours is a terribly long time when a man is love.- But he made up his mind to make the best of it; and in his heart he hoped that by then • the Duke and Duchess might have relented.

div.head: CHAPTER XX.
div.p: CHAPTER XX.

THROUGHOUT the day, wherever she turned, Bina found herself deliberately confronted -with Mr. Stuart in such a way as to confirm her suspicious of the matrimonial desires of her parents, and he seemed in -no way adverse and laid himself out to make himself pleasant. However, in her frame of mind she was not prepared to appreciate his efforts, and after iunch' alleging an imaginary headache, she took herself off to her room to indulge in a luxury of a good think about her lover, the present situation, and the happy prospect of the future.- To her temperament opposition was a goad, rather than a deterrent, and if the Duke and Duchess of Hampstead had only read their daughter's character more clearly or seen her pursed lips, as she sat thinking, it might have had an effect upon their im- mediate plans. But they were buth too full of an idea, to which they had abandoned themselves and their better judgment, to realise some of the most prominent obstacles in the way of its consummation. • Between three and four Charlie bounded into her room after a cursory knock. " Just off to Aldershot for guest night," he said. "So dropped in to say good-bye to you, old girl." He gave her an affectionate kiss. 'Can you spare me a moment, Charlie ? " she asked, a little shyly. "Just a moment," he said, looking at his watch. "The car is at the door, and I've promised to take Stuart for a run. I wish he could snare the evenino- and come down to

en from the aws to The !owe! tare; 17rfo seating himself at one end of it with the duke opposite nearest to the door. Ellis Gordon, in Frazer's absence, read the minutes, which Otto signed and the duke countersigned. " The first business of the 'evening, your Majesty, is to call upon the Earl of Portcullis to report." Otto motioned to the peer in question who rose a trifle unsteadily. , All the boyish bonhomie and cheeriness had left his manner and he was a very different creature from the well set up man of nerve of 'the previous week. "Your Majesty," he began, in a hoarse, halting voice, I did it—l did it, as ordered He never suspected, and I—well, I stabbed him on the Heath not far from Imre. He was going straight off to inform," he went on, gaining confidence as he proceeded; " so that there was no time to be lost. I carried him off to Shepherd's Bpsh and threw him into a garden. I took no risks, and I'm sure nobody can suspect anything." The eyes of all round the table glistened at his recital. The lust of blood was growing on them, and familiarity had taken the place of horror. Only Otto felt a little sick at the idea, but he had nerved himself to go through with it and saw that it was inevitable. "For Rudy's sake," he murmured, to .strengthen himself; and even Mr. Brinckley had not the courage to protest, as he leant forward with twitching mouth. Portcullis half sank, half fell back into his chair, his lower lip hanging loosely and his eyes fixed on some imaginary object in the corner. "It was inevitable," said Otto, in a low, half-apologetic voice; " and it- could not have been better done. We congratulate you, Lord Portcullis." Lord Portcullis, however, 141ardly seemed to hear. L "The next business if the evening, your Majesty," said the cliike, rising hastily, " is to draw lots in case of 'Lord Ben Nevis's refusal." All the eyes round the table again ,glistened. though one 'or two faces blanched with the !ear of drawing the fatal lot. - "Your Grace," began Otto. speaking sharply, "I beg of you, cannot this be avoided ? It is so—so terrible, so cold- blooded." The, duke's face flushed. He was 21311CritSfi

is not I whom you greet, I know and feel, but the rightful king in my person, and in this I comprehend your loyalty all the more—in that you were ready to lay down your lives for the King and the right without having seen him. This proves the depth of your loyalty to one who will ever be grateful to You all, come what way 1 We are but at the beginning of a difficult and dangerous time, the time of action, which may cost us not only our lives, but may bring opprobrium . •

upon your names when -dead-1-not the mere opprobrium of failure, but the taunt of treason. Dear friends, you have gone far, very far, for our sake, but remembe the Stuarts are an ill-fated and unlucky race. There is stitl, perhaps a chance of drawing back. Will you not take it and let me return to comparative obscurity rather than risk the valuable lives of those I love? Will you not take it I ask ? " "No, no," cried the Duke of Hampstead from his, distant seat, and his cry was taken up on every side. "There is no chance," muttered Lord Portcullis gloomily. His eyehs were blood. shot, and he looked as though he had beer drinking heavily. He spoke to himself, and nobody seemed to notice him, except Ather• Icy, who eyed the man of broken nerve with a strange curiosity. "Dear friends," continued Otto, warming to his subject, " I did it but to test you. I asked the question to see whether any amongst you wavered or regretted—to offer a chance of withdrawal to any who would. I would not lead unwilling men " Otto's voice grew very solemn —" perhaps to death. But as we are all agreed, all one, I can but heartily thank you from the very depths of my soul for your loyalty to King Charles 111., whose endeavour will ever be tc rule justly and generously from the throne of his fathers, should God grant success to the right. Dear friends, in return, I ask to be allowed to pledge you all and thank you foe your loyalty." Otto raised his glass and drained it, bowing to the company with an easy air of grace. Again there was a disposition to cheer, which had to be suppressed, and then the gathering resolved itself once more into a ;ocial one tor the time being. "The first ' King's Speech,' " murmured Carruthers, who had recovered his cynicism Half an hour later the Duke of Hampstead rose. "With your Majesty's permission," he said "we will now get on to business." . . -
Ottp assented : and the comnany

at otto's correction ana, even more so, at Tile want of nerve in Du blic. May I point out to your Majesty," he answered in his coldest voice, "that these precautions are inevitable for the sake of your own safety, the safety of all of us, and the . security Of the cause ? These considerations place the question of taking the life of an individual upon a totally different ethical basis to the ordinary one; and once it has been decided to invite anyone here to join the cause, it is a necessity that he should join us or—be silenced. As far as possible, in form- ing this committee, we have endeavoured to avoid asking anyone whom we did not think either certain of joining or vital to your cause. In the present instance I, personally, am particularly sorry that the Earl of Ben Nevis has been approached, as, apart from private reasons, I think that the,committee is perhaps quite large enough. However, it is now too late to question what has already been done. Our hope is that he will be lnval to the memory of his ancestors, who laid -down their lives and lost their estates in the '45. No man should have the Stuart cause more at heart."

Otto bowed, facing the inevitable. "Proceed," he said through his dry lips. "Perhaps your Grace will, draw the lots? ' The urn was placed in front of the duke, and all eyes were fixed in fascin2tion upon it. (To be continued.)

With the object of attracting the masses, some of the workers in connection with Bold-street Wesleyan Church, with Mr. E. Plinston as secretary and Mr. T. Stringer as treasurer, have hitj upon lan i innovation n the shape of Saturday evening popular penny concerts. The first of the series was held last Saturday in the commodious schoolroom and was well attended. An enjoyable pro- gramme was submitted and was highly appreciated. Selections were rendered in creditable style by Master T. Barton's juvenile orchestra, and a flute solo by Mr. Taylor was well received. Miss Plinston feelingly sang " Good-bye " and" The last milestone "and Miss Miller gave "Mid the hush of the corn "and" Kathleen Mavourneen." Mr. Frank Hickman pleased the assembly with several humorous songs. Mr. T. Brough acted as accompanist. The concert was presided, over by Mr. James Dodds who delivered a short address. He said he was once taking the chair at a Saturday night concert at Bolton, when several thousand people were present, and yet Bolton was not much more than double the size of Warrington. He thought in Warrington they ought to be able to get up concerts equal to those elsewhere, and also to be sufficiently well-attended to fill a room like that one. He had been under the impression that the concerts were to be a new departure, but he had ascertained since he came into the room that they were really a revival of a movement by his dear friend, and a true friend of Bold-street, and of the Wesleyan Church, namely, Mr. S. B. Stringer, who was a true citizen. He (Mr. Dodds) hoped God would raise up in connection with the church, many men as honoured. (Applause). The Chairman having alluded to the anniversary of the death of Nelson, said he hoped they would have friends in Warrington who would help them to carry on the grani work which had been begun in the shape of these Saturday night concerts, which were a counter-attraction to the public house, and that was an excellent object. Some people thought there was something good in beer. A working man once said that after he had had two gills he could knock a house down. "Well," was the relyof another working man ,to whom he was speaking, Ido not know about knocking a house down, but I have been a teetotaller for seven years, and I have knocked two up." (Laughter and apptause). If they could induce the people to attend those concerts in preference to the public-house it would be a grand thing for tbe town generally. (Applause). During an interval the Rev. Joseph Manning, in briefly explaining the objects of the concert on behalf of the committee, said they would stick at nothing that wouldlegitimately lead them to success and be was glad to say theylwere well backed in the matter. They werelmuch indebted to the chairman who had come at great incon-

venience to give them his help, He had promised that for one of the concerts he would bring a first class party from Liverpool to give a whole entertainment. First the promoters aimed at providing a good entertainment on Saturday night as that was the" off night "for most of the workers of the town. They were endeavouring to meet the need for wholesome recreation, and he made no apologies when he said that the Committee who had the work in hand were connected with a Christian Church. Ile thought it was quite time that the churches woke up to the possibilities of Saturday night. (Applause.) Some people would say it was not the business `of the church to provide recreation, but he . begged to differ from them. Social insincts were human. They were part of the man, and he held the Church as a Church bad a mission to the whole man. (Hear, hear.) In providing a good entertainment they wanted to help men and women to keep straight ; to provide a counter-attraction to the public-house ; and to do something to help people in the battle of life. They were, he trusted, doing a good deal in their ordinary Church work. but they felt there was a need for something else. They wanted to come into closer touch with those especially who did not go to the churches and chapels. He believed Saturday night concerts would ho a means to that end, and that they would be able to help some to live a better life to fight the evils of drink and gambling, and do something ,to make the town better than it was. (Applause).

WIFE'S PATHETIC APPEAL. A pathetic case was held at the Borough Police Court on Saturday, when Annie Glover, of Cyril-street, was summoned by her husband, who asked for a sepatation order on the ground that she was an habitual drunkard. —Complainant said he had tried hard for three years to get his wife to reform, but it was no use. She was a good wife and a good mother when she was sober, and he did not wish to throw her on to the streets if he could induce her to be better.—Prisoner burst into tears, exclaiming, "I will be a better woman if you will give me a chance. I will let the drink alone.."— Eventually the magistrates adjourned the case for a month.

Padgate Wesley Guild. There was a capital attendance at the Guild meeting which was held in the Wesleyan School on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. F. Wright in the absence of Bev. W. Mellor. An interesting address was delivered by Mr. Drinkwater, of Man- chester, his subject "The optimism and pessimism of modern poetry." By quotations from Shelly, Tenny- son, Browning and other poets of recent date, lie showed the poet's disposition to hopefulness or despair. His recitation of the various passages selected was a feature of the address. He was heartily thanked cm the motion of Mr. B. Mason seconded by Alderman I3ennett.

div.head: [AIL Rican RESER.VED.3 ANECDOTES OF DISRAELI,
div.p: [AIL Rican RESER.VED.3 ANECDOTES OF DISRAELI,
LEWIS DIELVILILs., (duthor of" The Life of Thackeray," te.).

Perhaps there was no figure in the Victorian era around which so much romance has been woven as in• the case of Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beconsfield. This is not unnatural when the man's career is remembered. It is a great achievement for any man to rise to be Prime Minister of the British Empire. But it is aia event unprecedented in the annals of parlia- ment that, at a time when England was one of the most aristocratic of countries, the House of Commons practically a preserve for the sons of patrician families, and the only passports to society a title, a million, or a genius, a man without social position, without wealth, solely by force of character and personal qualifications, should have secured the blue ribbon of political life. It is, indeed, the one example in this country of a man becoming Prime Minister, not by influence, nor brought in on the wave of public feeling on some party cry, but because he was the man, head and shoulders above his rivals, in whom parliament and _people alike had confidence.

Yet there was a moment when, apparently, Disraeli's career hung in the balance. This was during the controversy between Disraeli and Peel, with regard to the famous letter in which the former applied for office, when in 1841 the latter undertook to form a government. No one has been able to explain how it happened that a few years after, Disraeli rose in the House of Commons and stated: "I never shall—it is totally foreign to my nature—make an appli- cation for any place." It is scarcely credible he could have forgotten the missive, and yet, if he remembered, it is inconceivable he would have uttered that denial, when denial must almost inevitably have been followed by exposure. Even in his extreme danger, the fates fought for their favourite. In the small hours of the morning following the debate, Peel searched in his study for the incriminating document. He could not find it! That indeed was Disraeli's greatest good fortune. It it had been discovered, it would undoubtedly have been read in the House of Commons, and then, to all intents and purposes, Disraeli's parliamentary career would have been abruptly closed. Such an exposure—the lie direct—must have spelt ruin, and not even he could have lived it down. He would have been discredited for all • time. A faint hope exists that when the authorised biography appears, this matter will be made clear, but, on the face of it, it seems extremely improbable. Disraeli's personal charm was great and his tact immense, if he could not convert his enemies, at least he contrived to. win over lukewarm friends. For instance, he was anxious to secure a, great marjority for the third reading of the Empress of India Bill. The whips told him Dr. O'Leary's vote was doubtful. Later in the day in the lobby he found himself behind the Doctor. He caught him up and placing a hand on his shoulders, said: "My dear Doctor, you gave me quite a start. When I saw you I thought for a moment it was ray old friend, Tom Moore." Need it be said that Dr. O'Leary voted for the bill?
DISDAELI ANI) GLADSTONE.

It seems so natural for even the fiercest political antagonists to be friends in private life, that it is surprising to learn that Disraeli and Gladstone maintained no social relations outside the House of Commons. Gladstone thought Disraeli " devilish " and did not hesitate to express his opinion: indeed recently there has been published letters that passed , on this very subject between these great parliamentarians. Disraeli no doubt often deliberately angered Gladstone; and once, when the latter had made a very passionate reply, thumping the table in front of him. Disraeli thanked the powers that be that the substantial piece of furniture lay between him and his redoubtable foe. Someone once asked Disraeli : " What is the difference between a misfortune and a calamity !" only to receive the apparently serious reply "If Glad- stone fell into the Thames, that would be a misfortune, but if anyone pulled him out I think that would be a calamity." Disraeli was not above a pun, and when Gladstone was staying as the guest of Lady Couper at Wrest Park, be remarked : " Doubtless he thinks that I, the wicked, will cease from troubling while he, the weary, is at Wrest." But the following is by far the best Disraeli-Gladstone story. A friend told Disraeli that at a theatrical supper-party the question was asked of all the girls : Which would they choose if they had to marry either Gladstone or Disraeli I All but one said Disraeli, and the exception to the rule was almost un- popular until she explained her choice : "Glad- stone, so that I might elope with Disraeli and break Gladstone's heart !" Disraeli was de- lighted, and at a Cabinet Council on the morrow —when Russia was being somewhat agressive those assembled were awaiting a belat ed Minister, he told the story. Lord Cairns was disgusted, and Disraeli, annoyed by that noble- man's lack of humour, avenged himself by post- poning the Council for two hours on the ground of their colleague's absence. Mark the sequel. The evening papers came but with posters : "War Imminent! Second Cabinet Council summoned !" All Europe felt the thrill—and 80 history is made I Who • shall deny the wit of Disraeli whether in the• House of Commons or in private life? Some of his remarks have become historic, as when, in a debate on the Corn Laws when Peel had made his voile face: "The Right Hon. gentle- man has caught the whigs bathing, and has. walked away with their clothes ';" or when he called Lord Derby " the Prince Rupert of -Parliamentary discussion :" " his charge is re-, sistless but when he returns from the pursuit he always finds his camp in the possession of the enemy ;' or speaking of an Irish Bill: "This is a measure of necessity, conceived in a spirit of conciliation." " When I meet a man whose name I cannot remember," he said, " I always give myself two minutes. Then, if it is a hope- less case. I always ask And how is the ' old complaint?' In these days neither wealth nor a pedigree avail," he remarked; " for the former the world is too rich, for the latter too knowing."

A man, whose qualities- as a friend were greater than those as a writer, sent Disraeli one of his books. " I will lose no time reading your book," the minister assured him. This am- biguous reply is matched by that of an American author, the recipient of a presentation copy under similar conditions. He wrote a letter to the author praising the work, but justified himself by his concluding sentence : " I am lying under a sense of obligation." )

COOLNESS, TACT, AND WIT. The Disraeli of early days was no less witty. He had quarrelled with his father—lsaac Disraeli of " Curiosities of Literature" fame—whom the late Lord Dufferin's mother was anxious to meet. One fine day Disraeli arrived with his father in his right hand so to speak. Setting him down in a chair, and looking at him as if he were some object of vertu of which he wanted to dispose, the younger man said in a somewhat sententious manner : "Mrs. Blackwood, I have brought my father. I have become reconciled to my father on two conditions : the first was that he should come and see you ; the second that he should pay my debts." This is an admirable example of the impudence and nonchalance of the man who announced that he stood for parliament " on his head," and is a worthy companion of the story told of the day when, as a young man, he was driving with Sir Philip Rose to Shrewsbury, where, at the General Election, he had been nominated as the Conservative candidate. As they neared the borough, Sir Philip noticed a large poster, stopped the carriage, and calling his friend's attention to it, remarked : "It is something about you." Disraeli read the words printed in large letters : " Judgement Debts of Benjamin Disraeli. Tory Candidate for Shrews- bury." Underneath was a list of debts upon which judgement had been signed. This he perused carefully. Then he turned to Sir Philip and said placidly : " How accurate it is ! Nov let us .go on or we shall be late." lie won the election !

Sometimes the joke was against Disraeli. He was at one time notorious for his bad dinners. When he was Chancellor of the Exchequer he invited his colleagues to a meal, but the soup was vile. " Disraeli." enquired one of the guests, " is the soup made from Deferred Stock ' Another (limier was wretchedly served. Toe fish was tepid, the meat half-cord, the bird chilly. The last straw came when the ice MIS brought in me/fing. " Thank goodness," ex- claimed someone, " there's something hot at last." It was the late Lord !Salisbury who re- marked that the world had realised there were three things from which mankind could lie,

escape--toota acne, auu taxanon, and Hr. Ben- jamin Disraeli. Disraeli had a tender regard for all women, hut this foaling,' navor lwd him into indiscirAtions- At a time when the Government was siourly expected to make a move against Russia, he wat seated at dinner next to an impulsively patrio- tic Princess, who said to him: I cannot im- agine what you are waiting for 2" His reply was, in a way, to the point: "Potatoes, at this moment, madam." His relations with Queen Victoria in the end, were as satisfactory as could -be desired. ShMisliked him at first, and it is said he removed her prejudice with the statement that lie had learnt how to become an effective orator by studying the Prince Consort's speeches ! This may or may not be true, but it is certain be did not disdain the use of flattery' to gain his ends, though he was never a mere courtier. " Gladstone addresses the Queen as if she were a public department; I like a woman ;" he once replied. The secret of his influence with his sovereign lay in the fact that in trifles he never forgot her sex, and in great affairs never appeared to remember it. , One great advantage Disraeli possessed. He ' was the husband of a rich, admiring and en- couraging wife. He married in 1839, when he was thirty-five years old, the widow of his erstwhile colleague, Wyndham Lewis. He had met her 'several years before, for the first time at Bulwer's. "A pretty little woman, a flirt, and a rattle; indeed gifted with a volubility I should think unequalled, and of which I can convey no idea," he described her to his sister. "She told me she liked silent melancholy men.' I answered that' I had no doubt if it" His wife's fortune gave Disraeli at once the position that was necessary to forward his ambitions and in time enabled him to pay off his debts; while hes sympathy helped him in the hours of defeat. One night, when he had to deliver a great speech, she drove him down to Palace Yard. Her finger had been caught and unshed in the carriage-door, but she did not tell him what had happened and was not released from her torture until he had left her, lest it should disturb him ! Such a wife naturally deserved and received loyalty. "I say, Disraeli, what on earth -did you marry that woman for ?" asked Bernal Osborne at a dinner table. A dead silence suc- ceeded the question, and with one accord every- one looked at the sallow and grim figure to whom it was addressed. Disraeli played with his wine glass for a while, apparently unmoved, then very slowly he lifted his glitttering eyes. "Partly for a reason," he said, measuring his words in the silence, "partly for a reason which you will never be capable of understanding—gratitude!" It was ill crossings words with Disraeli! Mrs. Disraeli knew her "Dizzy" had not married for love. "He did not love me when he married me," she said proudly; "but now he couldn't change me for any woman in the world." Disraeli declared it was the happiest day of his life when, having himself refused a peerage, Queen Victoria created his wife in her own right Lady Beaconsfield of Beaconsfield. "I do owe to that lady all I have eirer accomplished, because, she has sup- ported me by her counsels and consoled me by the sweetness of her disposition," he remarked during her lifetime; and some time after her death he said to Lord Malmesbury "I hope some of my friends' will take notice of me now. I feel as if 1 had no home. When I tell my coachman to drive Home,' I feel it is a mockery."

div.head: DANGERS OF LIVER CHILL.
div.p: DANGERS OF LIVER CHILL.
A Wakefield Mother's Experience.
WONDERFUL BILK BEAN CURE.

At this time of the year liver chill is a common ail- ment. Many things contribute to liver chill : wet feet, insufficient clothing, living in a damp house, or wearing damp clothes. Many serious ailments originate from liver chill. Bile Beans banish liver chill by toning uir the liver and nourishing it by so assisting digestion that the food taken is turned into rich red blood, thereby preventing the presence of disease. Mrs. Alma Laverack, of Bishopgate, Westgate-street, Wakefield says :—" I caught a chill, which settled on my liver, and for weeks I lay in bed utterly prostrated. I couldn't lift my head, and I suffered fearfully from headache and pains in the chest and shoulders. and In the sides and loins.

"After five weeks in bed I managed to get up with great effort, but I was so weak that I was unable to stand, and was so dizzy the walls of the room seemed to be turning round. WOMEN'S CHAT.
The Examiner, Saturday, October 2B, 1905.

come as a boon and a blessing to the impecunious girl or woman, who perchance has to make gowns th-t have seen better days do duty once again for dinner parties and dances, during the coming winter. These garni- tures—composed for the greater part of flowers, foliage, and ribbons, are so lightly and gracefully arranged as to give one the impression of being just blown together, and the long trails, reaching well below the knees, can be worn in any fashion preferred. The favourite mode however, is to place the large cluster on the left shoulder, and drape one or two of the shorter trails across the bodice, allowing the remaining trail to fall straight from the left shoulder. The improvement such an addition makes to a middle aged or elderly gown, is little short of marvellous, and though the more elaborate garnitures are costly, very pretty specimens can be obtained for five or six shillings. The industri- ous and ingenious home worker could build them her- self, so also could she the floral tiaras, which are enjoy- ing so great a vogue at the moment. All that one needs are wire, flowers, and foliage, and a supply of patience. It will be remembered that on the occasion of the Princess Gustavus of Sweden's marriage, Princess Patricia of Connaught designed and fashioned with her own hands the pretty.and becoming wreaths worn by the bridesmaids.

Heads and Tails.--The modish long straight stole, one end of which hangs straight down in front, the other being flung over one shoulder, is invariably finished off with a collection of tails, but apparently heads are not of fashion, an idea the generality of women will welcome with delight. Such ornamenta- tions (?) are undesirable in the extreme, simply barbarous in fact. In the matter of tails however, the fashionable furrier is just letting himself go. They are hung about coats, muffs, stoles, and wraps, so generously, that one can only marvel how enough tails can have been secured to go round. In the cheaper varieties art steps in, but the "made tail " is despised by the high-class furrier. Waistbelts.—Elaborate embroideries end designs appear upon most of the new waistbelts. Many of the embossed leather specimens have an oriental design, showing the figures of quaint, and grotesque animals, and these are enjoying a great vogue. Other novel waistbelts have a narrow breadth of fur inserted in the centre of the belt, which gives a finishing touch to the winter costume. For evening wear there are the most delightful belts, built of white silk elastic with floral embroideries worked in colours to match the gown with which these belts are to be worn. Some of the most becoming, to be donned with an all black toilette, are of black silk, closely covered with glittering sequins.

div.head: MADGE.
div.p: MADGE.
The Warrington of Cromwell's Days.

• The weekly meeting in connection with the League of Young Liberals was held on Monday evening. Mr. Joseph Hawthorn read a paper in which he depicted the Warrington of Cromwell's days, and described the part played by the town in the civil strife of that period. The circumstances which led to the outbreak were reviewed, and the essayist showed that War- rington became a rallying point for the Royalist adherents, owing to its unique geographical position, there being no other point where the Mersey could he so safely crossed. For two years the Earl of Derby held the town and the pass of the Mersey for the King. defeating the Parliamentary forces in a skirmish at Stockton Heath, and, by fortifying the town with rude mud walls, frustrated all attemps to take it for a time. Subsequently, when under • the command of Colonel M. Morris, the garrison, after gallant defence, capitulated to the Parliamentary forces, and the siege came to an end. Cromwell and his victorious army entered the town after defeating the Duke of Hamilton's forces, and the large and dejected company of Scotch prisoners were dismissed at Warrington and departed for their native hills. The paper concluded with an appreciation of Cromwell.— The meeting was presided over by Mr. Guest, and the discussion which followed the reading of the paper was taken part in by Messrs. H. Gray (hon. secretary), J. Gray, Ford and Tilling.—Votes of thanks were accorded to the Chairman and Mr. Hawthorn.

div.head: WOMAN'S REALM
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.

QUM:IV VICTORIA ,AS ARTIST. ! Mrs. Marrablc, the President of the Society of Women Artists, told a quaint little story of the late Queen Victoria, in her address delivered at the International Art Congress in Venice. Emphasising the value- of drawing and perspec- tive in every kind of painting, Mrs. Marrable said that once Queen Victoria regretted to her master, William Leitch, that, as she was return- ing to London, she would have no opportunity of sketching from Nature. "Why not paint chimney-pots, madam?" he replied, and at her next lesson she shewed him, to his great sur- prise, three sheets of paper covered with sketches of chimney-pots, with all their little de- tails, weather-stains, and colouring well carried out. A story with an excellent lesson in it for those ambitious and over-hasty aspirants who have vet to learn that genius is largely the art of taking pains.

div.head: ITSEITI. COAT AND SKIRT.
div.p: ITSEITI. COAT AND SKIRT.

Pictured in our illustration is a smart and use- ful coat and skirt. The material• in which it is achieved is a rough diagonal serge of a pretty russet-red shade. The short little bolero has a turn-down collar of black velvet, and hangs over a high corselet belt of the same beautiful mate- rial. The separate effect of • belt and bolero is

only apparent, for in reality the belt is attached to the coat, and forms a part of it. No trimming appears on the coat, with the exception of two cut pieces of cloth on the lower edge and six' handsome smoked-pearl buttons in black metal rims. Gigot sleeves terminate in turn-back cuffs of black velvet. The skirt is plain, slightly full round the hips, and has a panel front decorated with two rows of black velvet buttons. Round the bottom run two pieces of cut cloth similar to those on the bolero. A hat of white felt, trimmed with black velvet and black and red wings, com- pletes the costume.

div.head: GOSSIP.
div.p: GOSSIP.

It is perhaps not very generally known that a profession open to women is that of registrar of births and deaths. There are, however, quite a number of women who have taken up this work both in London and in the provinces, and it is an interesting point to note that women are equally eligible with men as candidates for these poste. A great deal of roughness, rudeness, and ill- nature exist now, writes "Lady Phyllis" in the Bystander, which would have shocked our grandmothers. Such manners as they would have regarded with horror are simply passed over with indifference. It is partly true that we do not take time to be polite, but never correct that we may not do so if we will. " Push "is a snore correct solution. A CONVERTIBLE GOWN.

A convertible gown is a most useful posses- sion, and at the present moment it is not at all difficult to contrive one that will look modish in either of its forms. Our present sketch gives a suggestion for such a gown, to be carried out preferably in black taffetas. The skirt is very simply made, having the fulness tuoked round the hips, and the flounce set on to the skirt by incans of tucks also. The bodice pouches slightly

over a high, well-draped belt. The revers are of embroidery. edged with minute black chiffon frills, the puffed sleeves being finished at the elbow with gauntlet cuffs to matth. The yoke and under-sleeves, of white chiffon laid in tiny pleats, are made bu a loose foundation, so that when desired they can be removed, and a low- necked chemisette of lace and sleeve ruffles to match can be substituted for evening wear. ON LADIES-IN-WAITING. It seems somewhat strange, says MAP., that the daughters of King Edward should have tic official ladies-in-waiting, as is the custom with the daughters of most reigning Sovereigns. But there are several ladies who act as attendant: in an unofficial capacity. Princess Victoria's are Lady Hillingdon, with whom she has often stayed at Overstrand Hall, Cromer, and Lady Musgrave, who has been her hostess at Eden. hall, in Cumberland. Then the Duchess of Fife has secured the willing services of Lady Cecilia Webbe and Lady Clementine Walsh; while the Marquise d'flau;.poul seems to divide her time between these two Princesses and Princess. Charles of Denmark, when that Royal lady in this country. TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

POULET EN CASSEROLE, MARSEILLAISE. Halve, seed, and break up lib. of ripe tomatoes, and put them on with a carrot and one small onion, peeled and sliced, a good bouquet, and a pint of chicken stock; bring this all to the boil, and simmer gently till quite tender. Meanwhile cut loz. of fat bacon and the same of ham into dice, melt loz. of butter in a casserole, and .lay in the bacon and a nice fowl trussed for roasting, and fry it till the latter is evenly and delicately browned, when you lift it out and keep it hot. Next lay an ounce of flour into the pan, and stir it over the fire till well blended, but little if at all coloured. Now crush the tomatoes, Szc., through a sieve, and add them, with their stock, to the roux thus prepared; return the chicken to the nan. covering down the latter very closely. It it ail just reboil, men araw it to tneside ana simmer it steadily for twenty minutes or so, till the fowl is quite cooked; then skim off all the butter you can and season to taste with salt and twnnet. Serve very hot.

div.head: TITE FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: TITE FREE CHURCHES.
REVIVAL TIMES.

The revival which burst out in Wales last pear does not yet seem to have spent its force, and religious leaders in England are looking forward to its spreading to their country. A remarkable account of what are quite Revival Times appears in this month's Free Church Chronicle, Where Mr. Bewley Weaver, the President of the Hanley Council, writes on "The Aftermath of a Mission." Some Christians are at times doubtful as to the permanent good done by United Missions, but this article seems to give very clear testimony on the subject. Last January Gipsy Smith, the fwell-known Evange- list of the National Free Church Council, held a mission at Hanley, during which quite 2000 persons passed through the Enquiry Rooms, •Ind over 600 pledges were taken.

div.head: FOLLOWING UP THE WORK.
div.p: FOLLOWING UP THE WORK.

"Immediately after the mission closed," says Mr. Weaver, "each of the churches in the town held a recognition service for the young con- verts, and the harvest gathered was at once garnered. Arrangements were made by the council for a united evangelistic service to be held every Saturday night in the different chinches of the town. It proved a phenomenal success. A few meetings only had passed before we had to confine them to the larger churches, as the attcn lance averaged 1000 people, and sometimes rise to 1500. Without a single break this service has continued right through the summer mmths."

RFMAIZKABLE EFFECTS. The writer proceeds to give some instances of the remark ebb e effects of this mission. For instance, the harvest at Berryhill was gathered in the very hottest weather without a drop of intoxicating liquor being given to the labourers, and this of the free choice of the men them- selves. _ . _

For some years past the National Free Church Council has been endeavouring to pro- vide literature of a high-class character which shall appeal not only to those connected with the Free Churches but those outside. They issue every month a magazine for localising— the .Free Churchman. Some remarkable testi- roc:Lies have come to hand showing how by this means those outside the ordinary Church influ- ences have been reached and blessed. For instance, a localiser at Stockwell says: "Through its pages two habitual drunkards were directly brought to the footstool of Christ, and are now in our congregation? One of the Councils in Wales, which has recently passed through such stirring times, writes : "During the Revival we have known nothing better to put into the hands of converts with the Bible."

div.head: GOOD PROGRAMME.
div.p: A GOOD PROGRAMME.

Advance copies of the Free Churchman for January have heed prepared, and certainly the issue is a magnificent one. Six beautiful por- traits in two colours of Free Church leaders are given away with this issue, and no doubt these will be framed in thousands of homes. With the specimen copy is issued the programme for 1906, to which practically all the leading Free Church writers contribute. The Manager of the Publication Department, National Free Church Council, Memorial Hall, London, will send specimen copies to any desiring to localise.

div.head: VETERAN LEADER.
div.p: A VETERAN LEADER.

A few days ago Dr. Clifford, the veteran leader, celebrated his sixty-ninth anniversary. It seems difficult to realise that Dr. Clifford can be close on seventy. The amount he is able to accomplish, and the energy he throws into his work are marvellous. An account of an average day spent by Dr. Clifford is contributed to the •A.nuary number ot the Free Churchman by Mr. t. Mudie Smith. Mr. Smith tells an amusing anecdote in connection with Dr. Clifford's travel- ling habit.

div.head: CLOSE MARGIN.
div.p: A CLOSE MARGIN.

"How closely his margins are cut a singlo instance will suffice to prove. Dr. Clifford had, at the time of my marriage, very kindly con- sented to conduct the service. The morning arrived, and at breakfast I was sufficiently com- posed to read the newspaper. This composure suddenly received a terrific shock. My eye caught a headline: "Dr. Clifford at Birken- head "—the town may not have been Birkenhead, I really forget its name—it was sufficiently distant to cause me the liveliest apprehension. I read the paragraph: "Dr. Clifford speaking at so-and-so last night," said, &c.. ktc. Last night! How in the world was he going to get to London in time to marry me? My faith saved my reason. He had said he would be at the church at half-past twelve, the time the service was to commence, and though I did not see how he could manage to do it, I believed he would. I knew he could not have returned to town after his speech the pre- vious night, RR the last train had left before the meeting could have commenced. I confess that when 12.20 came and he had not arrived I felt a slight shiver down my spine, but five minutes later he walked into the vestry "more than usual calm." "I had a fright when I saw how far away you were last night: I didn't know you were out of town," said I. "No. I didn't mean you to," said he. "I knew you'd get anxious. I caught the 7.30 up, and reached home ten minutes ago."

div.head: MODERN NONCONFORMIST HISTORY.
div.p: MODERN NONCONFORMIST HISTORY.

The Rev. C. Silvester Horne, M.A., who, in addition to his many many other works, is becoming quite an historian, has written a com- pact volume on " Nonconformity in the Nine- teenth Century." This is published by the National Free Church Council at ls. 64. Another volnme also recently published is likely to be very timely—" The Soul's Wrestle With Doubt," by Rev. F. B. Meyer, B.A.

div.head: DR. HORTON ON HIGHER CRITICISM.
div.p: DR. HORTON ON HIGHER CRITICISM.

In his wonderful volume," The Open Secret,' a cheap edition of which hasjust been issued at is. net, Dr. Horton has some timely words as to the effect of Higher Criticism on Devotional Bible Reading. The modern reader may demur, and knowing little or much of the eager and restless criticism which has been applied to the Bible. may ask whether the book is not dis- credited as a revelation, and deprecated as a manual of devotion. Let it therefore be observed once for all, that criticism does not and cannot in the least alter the Bible as a fact. Its sole work is to consider the dates and the authorship of the several hooks, and possibly to readjust the order of the parts and the development of the truths. . It can no more affect the intrinsic quality of the actual use of the Bible, than the architectural criticism of a great cathedral can alter the use of the building for worship."

div.head: NEW WORK FOR GIRLS.
div.p: NEW WORK FOR GIRLS.

In many of our larger towns there are thou sands of girls employed in shops, many of them living away from home. This is the condition of affairs at Bournemouth. In order to provide for girls of this class, the Free Church Council there has recently opened a magnificent home. In addition to rooms for ordinary members, accommodation is provided for the lodging and boarding of thirty girls. Whilst a good deal of this accommodation will be used by local girls, the Guild will gladly take girls from any part of the country who may desire a short time of rest and recreation at that lovely southern resort. The terms are exceedingly low—l Os. to 15s. a week, and application should be made to Miss Perry, Cambridge House, Richmond-hill. Bournemouth:,

div.head: RADIUM AND HELIOTROPIS7,I.
div.p: RADIUM AND HELIOTROPIS7,I.

The property possessed by plants of growing towards or away from the light is known as positive or negative heliotropism. And experi- ments have been tried by Malisch to determine whether the emanations of radium produce a like effect. Seedlings of lentils, peas, and vetches were exposed to radium rays, but no heliotropism .was observed. When, however, the radium was mixed with zinc blende. which under these conditions becomes phosphorescent, the seedlings bent round at right anglos towards it. lt has thus been shewn that radium produces heliotropism in an indirect manner.

div.head: ACETYLENE CARBON.
div.p: ACETYLENE CARBON.

The carbon formed by the incomplete ccm- Lustion of acetylene is dull and porous, and it is n good conductor of heat and electricity. It has the specific gravity 1'919 at the ordinary tern- mrature, and the heat of combustion at con- stant pressure and volume at 20deg. Cent. is 7,994 calories for 1 gramme, or 94,723 calories for 12 grammes. The corresponding figures for graphite are 7,831 calories, and for charcoal (made from sugar) 8,057 calories. The value of the new form is hence very different from that of amorphous carbon, but approrsimately the same as graphite. Henri Moissan finds, however, that it does not contain graphite, and this is con- firmed by William G. Mixter, who has investi- gated its properties. One gramme of it is capable of condensing 1 milligrarnme of dry air on its surface and in its pores, but it exercises no catalytic effect on gas reactions, as does char- coal. It only absorbs 01 per cent. by weight of moisture from the atmosphere, and when heated with sulphuric acid there is no odour of sulphur dioxide.

div.head: SOUND OF A SUNBEAM.
div.p: THE SOUND OF A SUNBEAM.

One of the most wonderful diseov'eries in science is the fact that a beam of light produces sound. According to Milling a beam of sunlight is thrown through a lens on a glass vessel that contains lampblack, coloured silk or worsted, or other substances. A disc, having slits or open- ings cut in it, is made to revolve swiftly in thid beam of light so as to cut it up, thus making alternate flashes of light and shadow. On put- ting the ear to the glass vessel strange sounds are heard so long as the flashing beam is fall- ing on the vessel. But a still more wonderful discovery has been made. A beam of sunlight is caused to pass through a prism, so as to produce what is called the solar spectrum or rainbow. The disc is turned, and the coloured light of the rainbow is made to break through it. Now place the ear to the vessel. containing the silk, wool, or other material: As the coloured lights of the spec- trum fall upon it. sounds will be given by (Efferent parts of the spectrum, and there- will be silence in other parts. For instance, if the vessel contains red worsted, and the green light flashes upon it. loud sounds will be given. Only feeble sounds will be heard if the red and blue parts of the rainbow fall upon the vessel, and other colours make no sound at all. Green silk gives sound best in red light. Every kind of material gives more or less sound in different colours, and utters no sound in others.

div.head: SOLAR CORONA.
div.p: THE SOLAR CORONA.

Sir R. Ball has described the result of recent discoveries concerning the sun in a lecture de- livered at the Bishopsg,ate Institute, London. There was, he said, around the sun a corona of pearly light, and it was one of the great enigmas of nature—what is the corona? During the last eclipse of the sun an attempt by co-operation on the part of astronomers to discover whether the corona changed in size had been frustrated by bad weather in Labrador. But the opportunity would recur. Mow was the sun's heat kept up? All the coal on the earth would not supply the sun's heat for snle-tenth of a second. But the sun was shrinkieg. Its particles developed heat by falling together. Li this way they could account for the sun's heat through 24,C00,000 years. But the geologist said : " What's the good of 24.CC0.CC0 years to me ? My phenomena want hundrods of millions." To which the physicist had retorted: "Then you must hurry up your phenomena." But the discovery of radium had 1..,ut an end to the ch,asllock. There were materials in the world, of which radium was one, w hich were continuall7 sending forth corpuscles with tremendous veloity. If there veto in the sun as much radium as the bulk of the earth, that is to say, 1-300,CCOth part of the sun, then, imtead of 24,C00,000 years, they had tt once I,CGO.OOO,CCO year: available for the life of the sun. That was probably the explination, and thus the discovery of radium had ,rought about the removal of one of the greatest diffi- culties that had over troubled science.

div.head: SIR W. CROOKES ON DIAMONDS.
div.p: SIR W. CROOKES ON DIAMONDS.

In a lecture on diamonds Sir William Crookei gave an interesting account of diamonds, where they were fonnd, and how they were made. He pointed out that whilst in Brazil and India dia- monds were worked from gravels, in South Africa they were found in pipes or shafts intes- smiting the country rock, generally dark shales and hard grits, with occasional masses of basalt. The pipes are all filled with a material that is soft and yellowish to a depth of about 80ft., then changes to a dull greenish or bluish colour, and gradually becomes about as hard as a lime- stone. It consists of rock fragments and mine- rals embedded in. a cement of carbonate of lime and serpentine. The rock fragments are mostly shale, grit, and basaltic rock, the minerals in- cluding, besides diamonds, garnet, brown mica, and iron ores, practically all being such as usually form at high temperatures and pressures.

div.head: DTPTPPLACE OF TIER GEIS.
div.p: DTPTPPLACE OF TIER GEIS.

The material filling the pipes, though some- what resembling that in the throats of extinct voleanoes. differs, like the pipes themselves, in some important respects. Though volcanic, in the sense of having been formed end filled by explo- sions. the agent, as Sir W. Crookes shewed. could only be water. gas, or something of that nature, suddenly released from great pressure deep below the earth's surface; and he illus- trated by results of experiments with explosives that the pipes could thus be made and filled. Diamond is one form of crystallised carbon, and it was at one time thought to have been pro- duced in the pipe itself. It is. however, now generally admitted that the birthplace of the gem, as of most of the other hard minerals found with it. was elsewhere. One fact is noteworthy, that the diamonds from different pipes are not absolutely identical, but shew individual charac- teristics, just sufficient to be recognised by an exnert. But

WHILST we are talking of Tun COST or NELSON, it may be well INEFFICIENCY, to consider whether we have learnt much since his day as to the proper method of conducting national affairs. NELSON was frequently at war not only with the enemies of his country but with the Government department to which he was immediately responsible. He owed very little indeed of his amazing success to the manner in which he was backed up by the Admiralty. It may safely be said, in fact, that no other man of any age could have accomplished NELSON'S resources. The money voted for the Navy in those days was only in part expended upon it, and the case has been the same ever since, Some years ago Lord CHARLES BERESFORD declared that in his opinion, and so far as his knowledge went, for every £lOO paid by the taxpayer for naval armament only £5O of value was received by the Navy. At about the same time he succeeded in alarming the country by shewing that the ' Admiralty had no plans for conducting a naval campaign. If war broke out we should have to "muddle through" according to some rule of thumb. In this respect there has, we believe, been a change for the be.;ter. There are plans in the Admiralty pigeonholes, at any rate, and public confidence in Sir JOHN FISHER is very much mis- placed if he has not introduced many economies and improvements into the spending department. Yet some things which take place suggest a doubt. When several of our obsolete ironclade were " scrapped" not long ago, it was discovered that large sums of money had been spent upon them for repairs. The fact that a vessel of war had become useless did not suggest to the authorities that to spend money upon it would be exactly equivalent to throwing ,that money away. Well-established routine does not permit such considerations as this to interfere. When, evidently on the advice of Sir JOHN FISHER, the Government dealt with the Navy as HAMLET advised his mother to deal with her heart—" Oh, throw away the worser half of it, and live the better for the other half! "—a perfectly wasteful and wanton expenditure came to an er.d. But for the energy and clear-sightedness of one strong man this waste might !lave gone on without inter- ruption for years to come, with the result of tinkering up year after year vessels that would be worse than useless in war time. As Mr. ARNOLD WHITE reminds us, the civil, military, and naval administration of Great Britain has no incentive to thrift. " No civil servant," he says, "is promoted or praised for preventing waste, or for devising a cheaper or quicker form of carrying out the national service." The con- trary is the fact. An energetic servant of the nation becomes simply an intolerable nuisance to officials of the Tite Barnacle species. He is a person to be got rid of as soon as possible, and by the nearest available way. But the more in- efficient the public service becomes—and it becomes inefficient through the crushing of all talent and initiative under the hard wheels of routine—the more it is certain to cost. The recently condemned ships are, again, a case in point. We are now spending some sixty millions a year more than we were when the Rosebery Government left office Arithmetical persons who desire to apprehend. more vividly what this means may divide up the sum by weeks and days. The great bulk of this increased expenditure has gone to the Army and Navy. As to what has happened to the Army under a regime of greatly increased costliness, we have positive knowledge. The Army has at last "gone to the dogs," as has been so often prophesied of it. If its services were required on any great scale they would not be available. Nobody would know what to do. There would simply be a repetition of the confusion which prevailed when, during the Boer war, we had to strip the Navy of ammunition in order to equip the land forces. That the Navy is all right almost everybody believes. That is an article of the popular faith ; and certainly the Navy ought to be if money could make it so. The demands . for naval expenditure are becoming so large that they must before long be felt as a crushing burden. A change of Govern- ment is even less desirable on political grounds

of economy, efficiency, and national re-organisation No reasonable Englishman will feel quite safe so long as his Majesty's present advisers' remain in office. They have increased the expenses of government beyond what had ever previously been dreamt; and what they have given us in exchange for an immense increase in the taxation of the country is a general sense of insecurity.
A month ago the THE CHARGES Town Clerk announced AGAINST COUNCILLORS. to the Town Council

that his application to the Attorney-General for leave to proceed against two Councillors under the Corrupt Prac- tices Act, was the only document in connection with the case that he proposed to lay before them Tins dictum was in complete variance with a previ- ous understanding that the actual statement of the case should be submitted to the Council before being forwarded to the Attorney-General, and it naturally caused great dissatisfaction. The Investigation Committee which inquired into the charges in the first place was quite within its ,ights in demanding to see the statement of the case as prepared by their legal adviser, the Town Clerk, and the Council as a whole expected a similar indulgence to be shown in the matter. As a sequel to the impasse created by the Town Clerk's attitude, Councillor Lord will move on Tuesday a resolution in the name of the Town Council calling upon the Town Clerk to lay the statement of the case before the Investigation Committee prior to it being submitted to the Attorney-General. This is, we cousider, quite a legitimate and reasonable claim, and we hope in the best interests of the town and the gentlemen implicated that there will be no demur.
There is no Out- THE MumarAL ELECTIONS. standina feature

of the November elections in Warrington this year and only three contests will take place. Liberals and Tories are not in such active opposition as formerly, and the Non-Traders are not making any special effort. Yet all three parties have candidates in the field, so that the position of matters is not without interest. Apparently, the Non-Traders stand to gain most, for every one of the six candidates is, we understand, either a supporter of the Non- Trading cause or in sympathy with it. The Liberals have an official candidate in each of the three wards to be contested, viz. : Mr. Pickavance 'in Howley, Mr. Peacock in Bewsey, and Mr. Critchley in Town Hall Ward. A strong effort has been made to obtain good Liberals to contest for municipal honours this year, in order to test and strengthen the party machinery, and these three candidates will, we hope, in the. Liberal interest be awardad a full measure of party sup- port. We quite agree with tte contention often advanced that it would be far better were politics rigorously eschewed from municipal elections, but the difficulties in the way of contesting the elec- tions on purely independent lines are almost insur- mountable. Even were the Liberal and Conserva- tive parties to agree not to interfere in municipal matters, the presence of the Labour group would complicate tha situation. Then there is the undeniable fact that so long as party rivalry exists in any shape or form, there will be party divisions in the local Parliament, and a trial of strength iuovitable. It appears to us that candida. es will always have to be weighed in the political balance, and so long as their colour is pronounced we think it incumbent on party men to support the party nominees. We therefore exhort all Liberals in the three contested wards to plump for the Liberal candidates on Wednesday next.
