div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE.
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE.

_ to Captain Crosfield for replies to our leaderette last week on the question of national service as applied to nationl defence. Their attitude and views are, of course, : not a matter for speculation. As National Service Leaguers, they conceive the "whole duty of man'' —or his primary duty at any rate—to be to bear arms in defence of his country, and if he declines for what may be adequate reasons to himself then he must be compelled. He may be a Quaker, and look upon the dread arbitrament of war as a crime second not even to those we are abjured against by Divine command, and yet if the 1, National Service League proposals become law, he must shoulder his gun and obtain the necessary qualifications for killing his fellow-man by the quickest and most expert method. Miss Cree- -1 field argues with force and logic in favour of man's duty to the State, and we I venture to pay her the compliment that she has stated the case for national service as eloquently and convincingly as we believe it can be put. But on ethical grouuds we still contend that to impose military training on- the men of the country is au interference with constitutional doctrine and the freedom of action and thought in the individual. The fact that the education of our children and the payment of rates are compulsory on us all does not, in our view, bear very closely upon the claim for individual freedom. Civilization itself demands the construction and observance of certain social and moral laws, but we do not see how this can be fairly construed into an augument for compulsory military training. It might just as reasonably be urged that the attendance of everyone at some place of worship should be com- pelled by the State for the good of the community. We think that the right of every man and woman to act as conscience dictates in either imperial or personal affairs should remain absolute and not be wantonly assailed

Leaving the ethical standpoint and coming to the sphere of practical politics we still dispute the assertion that any necessity has arisen for the introduction of compulsory military service. The inefficiency of the army and its auxiliary services is a status quo which can be taken as a basis of agreement. From it the Di etional Service Leaguers obtain their chief argument for the proposals they expound. We see in it only an all-sufficient reason for a re-organization of the system which governs both the standing Army and the forces which volunteer for service as defenders of the country. He the utmost been done to make either branch 'of the military establishment efficient P We ail noP and we contend that National safety could be assured as easily by a wise, and proper encourage- ment and control of both services a 3 by compulsory military training. So far we have met with no argument which disposes of this contention or shakes our belief in the efficiency of a citizen force voluntarily enlisted. Make the army a paying profession, and give the volunteers their due, and we shall have no need to consider inch a sub- versive proposal as that of the National Service League. '

Sunday has been set apart by the clergr men and ministers of all denominations responsible for the movement 019 the day upon which the citizens of the United . Kingdom shall be exhorted from the pulpit to do their duty. The occasion should afford splendid • opportunities, beset though it must be, in the . natural order of things, with temptations to travel outside the sphere which the phrase i Citizen Sunday sugests to the possessor of the ordinary workaday mind. It is, surel3:o possible, without introducing any question 0' 1 doctrine—without, in fact, "beating the drain 'ecclesiastic "—to preach a code of commercial morality which shall make for the maintenance of the mercantile supremacy ot the Empire. The pitfalls which encompass the situation can have 0? 1 terrors for those counsellors whose singte-mindeo ' I aim is to convince their congregations that, not' 1 withstanding the prevalent cynicism of the times, 1 honesty is the best policy, in the home in the , workshop, and'in the mart. Effective sofeconitY may, we opine' be given to such a pronouncement, as this without the introduction of controversis matter anent tenets. "Do your duty as a goo"' citizen," seems to is an all•sufficient text from which to preach sermons which will sink deep ia° the hearts of the listeners,without the adventitious aid of the odium thelogicum. div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The Town Council meets at 6 p.m. on Tuesday next —the day before the elections. What is it we want that thp Atabour party cannot get for us ?" said a lady speaker 'in Manchester to a crowd of workers this week. "Can they get us husbands ?" was the answer.

_ " More kicks than halfpence " is the usual reward of the Town Councillor, according to Alderman Tinnion. But then there is always the hope of an aldermanic seat with its social status, turtle soup, and reduced anxiety.

* * * " The crying need of the day is greater kindness between women, a truce to their jealousy, their Pettiness, their want of generosity. Men, with all their faults, are finer human beings,better Christians." A correspondent in" Woman." * * * A novel contest will take place at Bury St. Edmunds at the municipal elections. The Mayor ha 3 resigned Ins position in order to contest an election against the late Town Clerk, who resigned recently owing to differences with the Council. This ought to be what is known as a spicy fight. * * * Liverpool municipal Candidates have been asked to get a bye-law passed, making ultra-amorous courting and kissing in public places subject to a fine of £2 and costs. Bye-laws against flirting —about which we heard so much in the " Mikado " last week —will perhaps be next in demand. * * * At a meeting of the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council, under the presidency of Sir John Brunner Bart., M.P„ it was reported that for the first time in the political history of Cheshire there are Liberal candidates for every seat in the county, and it was 'confidently predicted that, the next election will see Cheshire returning a majority of Liberal members.

" Could there be found in any land, in any clime, sim hundred women who—even under the leadership of such a graceless, golfing " Gallio " afk the present Prime Minister—could possibly contrive to do as much mischief and inflict as much wrong upon the flatiron as have the six hundred members of Parliament recently assembled at St. Stephens ?" " Iconoclast " in the " Daily News."

* * * Cmncillor Clegg says he is convinced that too much of the ratepayers monl is being spent to push private ends. This is a topic that should not be held back, and we hope Councillor Clegg will take an early opportunity of redeeming Ins promise to enlarge up- on the subject. We had thought axe-grinding was in disfavour at the Town Hall, but if it still goes on there we trust Councillor Clegg will exert himself to expose it.

* * Any movement to provide wholesome Saturday night recreation for the masses is to be commended, and we wish every success to the series of popular 'Penny concerts inaugurated in connection with Bold- street Wesle)an Church. The opening last Saturday was most encouraging and when it becomes more widely-known that for such a trifling sum one can enjoy a capital entertainment, public support should realize all expectations. * * A man in India found a rattlesnake wedged in by a rack, which threatened its destruction. He removed the rock, releasing the snake, which showed obvious Signs of gratitude. He took the snake home with him, and kept it for months about the house, where it seemed absolutely free from danger. One night he was aroused by a noise. Going to discover the cause, he found the snake coiled round a thief, while its tail was out of the window rattling for the 'police! And yet snakes have a poor reputation for gratitude!

* * * A new inducement to school attendance has been Offered in the States. One of the rural schools in Kansas has a pretty girl as its teacher, but she was much troubled at first because many of her pupils were late every morning. At last she made the announcement that she would kiss the• first pupil to arrive at the school-house the next morning. At sun- rise (according to the "New York Tribune ") the Three largest boys in her class were sitting on the doorstep of the school-house, and by six o'clock every bov in the school and four of the directors were wait- .. . lng for her to arrive. We wonder how the idea ___ _ .
would work on this side of the herring pond.

. * * * . It is gratifying to see that the University Extension lectures arranged by the Education Committee are being well supported by the townspeople. Students of literature 03u1d not do better than avail themselves of these opportunities of becoming more fully acquainted with the lives and work of three great essayists—Lamb, Hazlitt and De Quincey. The lecturer, the Rev. W. Lawrence Schroeder, MA., • treats his subject most interestingly,his remarks being illumined with many delightful humorous touches. A i tribute to his ability is the fact that last Friday l evening,with the fullest encouragement of the audience, ~ he was able to continue the lecture for quite twenty ( . ininutee beyond the period usually allotted. i: Our hearty thanks to the genial "Teddy " and pros- f4 ' pective Councillor Pickavance. Many a time and oft we have complained of the disgraceful street-paving in Warrington and unhesitatingly given it the distinc- tion of being the worst paved town of any size we knew. Mr. Pickavance was busy charming the ears of the Howley Ward electorate on Wednesday evening when he backed our assertion. As a wheel-man he can speak with aulhority, and when he says that Knuts- ford-road, Wilderspool-road and Winwick-road are unfit for any self-resnecting cyclist to ride along "he is to be believed. They are, and the block-paved portion of Sankey-stieet is worse ! If we had a vote ic Howley Ward Vie should unhesitatingly give it to Mr. Pickavance as a sort of palliative for saddle soreness. * * * Heywood Conservatives must be feeling very sore Over a blunder which has placed them in the position of having no candidates nominated to contest the municipal elections on Wednesday next. The result is that Councillor Thomas Popple, the leader of the Unionist Party in the Heywood Parliamentary rsivision, Councillor C. Cook, who is the vice-chair- man of the Heywood Education Authority, and Councillor David Arnott, the three Conservative candidates who retired, lose their seats. The extra- , ordinary blunder, it is officially stated, is due to the fact that the Conservative agent was under the impres- sion that the nomination day was Wednesday instead ot Tuesday and therefore no papers were handed in. ii 110futche heclaencdtiiodnatleits bad,eraturebehenadisbsueeeldi .prepared on behalf `. of the Conservative Party, and the election addresses * * « used to see the following in the

-ple British Bandsman " of October 21st grand 'lnstance of what should be a general ' occurrence after a contest instead of an exception, has just been brought before our notice. Crostield's soap works band and Slaithwaite band competed in the grand Rhield section at the National Band Festival, but Cros- field's were placed second to Slaithwaite, who were warded premier honours by the judges. Almost immediately after the event a letter was received by the secretary to Filaithwaite from Crosfield's, in which the latter heartily congratulated the former on their Splendid win at the Crystal Palace. The letter goes on to say You certainly gave a first class per- formance. Of course we are sorry we could not beat Y(311, but we think it a most fair de:iision and the best 'band won on its merits.' This is tho sort of feeling We have always advocated. Too long and too often have the results of contests caused bad blood and ill will and the generous action of the splendid Lanca- shire band may be commended for adoption by all who have occasion to be connected with band mil- -testing."

Notice. The Warrington " Examiner " is now published on i Friday afternoon, price one penny, and s on sale at the various newsagents at about 4 o'clock. Should any difficulty be experienced in getting the paper the proprietors will undertake to deliver a copy at any address in Warrington by 5 o'clock on Friday after noon without extra charge. Address all communica- tions to "Examiner Office," Bewsey-street Warrington

ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Coming Events. A four-days bazaar in connection with St. James' Church, Latchford, will be held in the schools next Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday. On Wednesday it will be opened by Mrs. Frost, Grappen- hall Hall. Mrs. Fielding Ould, London, will perform the ceremony on the second day while on Friday and Saturday respectively Mr. J. Littler,Runcorn,and Mrs. F E.Powell, Sewerby, will officiate. In addition to the usual attractions of a bazaar concerts will be held at frequent intervals. Particulars as to prices &c., will be found in our advertising columns. -

The third of the course of University Extension Lectures will be given in the Co-operative Hall on Friday next by the Rev. W. L. Schroeder, NIA., on 'The Essays of Elia " and "The life and Personality of William Hazlitt."

The annual sale of work in connection with St. Peter's Church will be held in the schoolroom, John- street, on Monday and Tuesday next. The Mayor will open the sale on Monday, and Mrs. Frost will perform that ceremony on Tuesday. " Cristian Citizenship " will be the Rev. H. Dunnico's subject a thel Parr Hall service on Sunday evening. An open meeting of Wycliffe P.S.A. Society will be held on Sunday afternoon. Mr. J. W. Slack will pre- side and the speaker will be Mr. J. Walley, of Man- chester. The Warrington Apollo Quartette Party will sing. _ •_ _

The new Wesleyan Methodist Church and School at Stockton Heath will be opened on Thursday afternoon next by Miss Bessie Dutton. A special sermon will be preached by the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones, of Man- chester. In the evening a public meeting will be held at which Mr. C. E. Parker will preside. At the Warrington Police Court to-day (Friday), John Horsfall, 14, Gladstone street, was charged with stealing from the London and North-Western Railway Company at eleven o'clock on Saturday bight, twelve bottles of whisky, the property of the company. Mr. Lindon Riley, barrister, appeared to prosecute.—Mr. Steel on behalf of the prisoner 'admitted the theft and made a strong appeal for leniency, on the ground of the prisoner's previous good character, he having served the Company faith- fully for 23 years.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for three mouths with hard labour. Recent Police Charity Sports.

As a result of the above sports, the net proceeds amount to the substantial sum of £6B 15s. 81d. From this sum £34 Bs. will be donated to the Infirmary, £l7 14s. to the District Nurses Association, and £l7 3s. 81d. to tie Police Athletic Club. During the past nine years the club, through its annual fete days have donated to the Infirmary, and District Nurses Association, the sum of £527 I3s. Id. Exciting Scene in Bridge-street.

An exciting scene was witnessed in Bridge•street about 8 o'clock on Monday morning. A horse attached to a spring cart belonging to the executors of the late Mr. J. Blackshaw, farmer, Hatton, Cheshire, was pro- ceeding along Horseruarket-street, when it took fright owing to the bridle being loose. It galloped down Bridge-street and when at the corner of Rylands- street, ran into a coal lorry belonging to Mr. William Timmins, of 50, Slater-street, knocking the horse down. The shafts of the lorry were broken and the coal scales damaged, Timmins receiving injuries to his fingers. Mr. Blackshavr, who was driving the frightened horse, succeeded in jumping out of the cart at Market Gate and escaped without injury.

" The Gems." " The Gems" concert party will visit Warrington on November 7th and Bth when they will appear in the Parr Hall. The entertainment promises to be an unusually attractive one, great and pleasing variety distinguishing the programme. The party consists of Miss °Elsie Jones (soprano), Miss Olive Mortimer (contralto), Mr. Kenna Lawson (humorist), Mr. Wallace Kennedy (tenor), Mr. Edgar Stevens (baritone), and Mr. Harold Scott (solo pianist), who both individually land collectively are most capable entertainers. Wm. Benson (C.N.T.)° James Critchley (L.) Peter Peacock (L.)* James Dickenson (I.) E. Pickavance (L.) Thos. Chan* (C.) Denotes retiring Councillor. MR. PEACOCK'S NOMINATIONS.

Mr. Peter Peaoock has probably established a record with regard to the number of nominations sent in on his behalf, no fewer than 23 hiving been received.
TOWN HALL WARD.

On Tnesday afternoon Mr. James Critchley, White- field-road, Stockton Heath,was nominated as the Liberal oandidate for the above ward in two papers, His pro- poser in the first paper VMS Mr. George Wallington, and his seconder Mr. William Beswick. and the assenting burgesses were Messrs. William Hewitt Dutton, George Gilley, Walter Richard Smith, Joseph Herbert Morton, Thomas Critchley, William Patrick, William Jones, and David Lowe, In the second paper the proposer is Mr. John Wilkinson and the seconder Mr. Patrick O'Brien. POINTS FR,031 ME CANDIDATES' ADDRESSES.

In his address to the electors of Town Hall Ward, ; Mr. James Critchley says he would support the , strengthening of the bye-laws s!la that all streets and . passages should be nude beford any house is tenanted. He would support more open spaces in all the Wards, or the use of day school yards 113 playgrounds, and he is also in favour of municipal bowling greens. Other measures which Mr. Critohley bays he would support are the fair wage clause in all contracts,. a living wage to Corporation woakmen, and a reduction of the price of gas. Mr. William Benson says he is not the nominee of any private individual, nor has he any private interests to serve; indeed, his entry. into the 'Council has meant I a considerable loss to him an many ways, owing mainly to his sympathy with those who have so strenuously opposed any member making anything from his position. He will continue to act on those lines, regardless of all consequences. Owing solely to the work of the Non- Trading members of the Council the rates (apert from the education rate) were this year reduced aid. in the 2 and, with Councillor Burton. he anticipates a further reduction next year. The charge for gas to consumers lis too high considering the profit made. He voted tar a reduction this year and he says, will do so again. I Mr. Edward Pickavance informs the Howley Ward electors that he is a large ratepayer and 'property owner 'in the ward, so that he has some Interest at stake. He is in favour of lower rates, better paved and lighted , streets and passages, cheap gas, and better houses for I the working claeses. He is strongly in favour of pro- voiding a recreation pound for the children of the t Ward, and would also like to see the wider streets planted with trees, so as to make the Ward rather more ' attractive than it has hitherto been. His best efforts will be devoted to secure the strictest possible economy in municipal expenditure coupled with efficiency and progress. Mr. Thomas Chantler urges the neeessity of a play- ground for children in the Ward and a reduction of the price of gas. He is not, he says, fighting the election on personal grounds. All he desires is pure and honest government and he believes Li a living wage for workingmen. Mr. Peter Peacock, in his address to the burgesses of Bewsey Ward, says most of the reforms he has proposed while in the Council have been agreed to, amongst them being free admission to the baths for school children. Workingmen can also have tickets at a reduced price. He refers to the great progress which has been made in the paving of steeots and passages, pointing out that he has acted as a member of the committee which has had the work in hand. He is in favour of a further reduction in the price of gas, and also of id. tram fares, end he disaerees with the action of the Education Com- mittee in excluding children under fire from school. Other matters which will have his support are free breakfasts for needy school children, better housing for the working classes, and all measures for the interest and betterment of the working classes. Mr. James Dodds has issued a letter in support of the candidature of Mr. James Dickenson who, he says, he has known for many years as a worthy citizen of the highest character who pays his way and has the respect of all who know him as a thoroughly reliable man, and as One who would do his utmost for the rat ep ayers without making promises which canuot be carried out. Mr. Dodds says he believes the ratepayers will be act- ing in the best interests of their families, themselves, and the town be returning a good and tried men snch as he believes Mr. Dickenson to be. MR. DODDS AND PARTY POLITICS.

On our front page will bp found a manifesto to the electors from Mr. James Dodds on the subject of party politics in municipal elections, and containing a vigor- ous denunciation of the action of the Liberal execu- tive.

div.head: AFFRAY AT SANK.
div.p: THE AFFRAY AT SANK.
Adjourned Inquest.

Coroner Brighouse held the adjourned inquest at the Police Station this (Friday) morning, touching the death of John Flemming, farm labourer, who, it was alleged, received fetal injuries in an affray at Sankey. Four Irish farm labourers named Petrick Norma, Thos. Cunniff, John Laheel and Michael Garrity were in custody on the charge of wilfully murdering the deceased. Mr. A. Browne appeared on behalf of the priFoners, Superintendent Strickland for the County police and Mr. T. S. Steel for the licensee of the Butcher's Arms. The dying depoQitions of the decewei were nit taken in strictly legal form and were therefore ruled to b 3 inadmissible.

A post mortem examination by Drs. Smith and Braide showed that death was due to peritonitis brought on by a rupture of the bowls. thth decOrs were of the opinion that the rupture was caused by a kick. It was proved that Laheen, Garrity and Flemming were in the Butcher's Aims when about ,fifteen farm labourers were ordered out for quarrelling. The disturbance was renewed outside, and, it was alleged, Flemming was kicked but the police cauld produce no evidence to show that the prisoners were concerned in the affray.. . . . .
After a- long inquiry the jury returned a verdict that Flemming died from injuries receivi.d, under what circumstances there was no evidence to show.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.

The birth-rate was equal to 293 The death-rate from all causes was equal to 135 per 1,000 against 14.0 the average of the previous 4 weeks and against 13.7 the corresponding period of last year. The death rate from the seven chief z.vin n tic diseases was equal to 07 per 1,000, against 4.1 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 22 the corresponding period of 1904. The ages of mortality were:- 0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65—up. Total 2 3 1 10 2 18.

The deaths included-1 from whooping couch, 2 from influenza, 4 from phthisis, 1 from cancer, 2 from lung diseases, 8 from all other causes. The following cases of infectious diseases have been reported during the week :—Scarlet fever, 3 cases, diphtheria, 2 cases. The maximum temperature 49 F., was recorded on the 21st inst., and the minimum temperature 27 F., on the 18th net. The rainfall measured '9 inch. The general direction was E.N.E.

div.head: CORRECTION.
div.p: A CORRECTION.

In our report of last wesk of the mating held in the Co-operative Hall, Winwick-street, in support of the candtdatore of Mr. P. Poscock we stated that Councillor Wright seconded a resolution of support The seconder of the resolution was Mr. S. Wright J.P.

MR. E. PICKAVANCE'S CANDIDATURE. MEETING IN THE NATIONAL SCHOOLS. On Wednesday evening a meeting in supptrt of the candidature of Mr. E. Pickavance in Howley Ward was held in the National Schools, Church-street. There was a large and enthusiastic gathering over which Coun- cillor William Clegg presided. There was also present on the platform : Mr. E. Pickavance,Alderman Tinnion, Messrs. S. Wright, E. Wynne-Jones, A. Booth, James Looker, and W. H. Sherburn. I The CHAIMIAN took the opportunity of reviewing ' his work as a representative of Howley Ward in the Council during the past year. He referred to the different committees with which he is connected and pointed out that altogether he had attended eighty meetings, exclusive of sub-committees. With regard to contracts, he had been desiroas that as fares possible the principle should be that all work that could be done in:Warrington should be done here.On one occasion there was a Warriugton tender of about £609, which, how- ever, was not the smallest. He and two other Coun- cillors, however, pressed that the order should be given to the Warrington firm, pointing out that the difference between that contract and the lowest would be covered by the cost of carriage, corres- pondence, Ste., and eventually the committee agreed to that course. When he was, returned to the Council he found the system of supplying food to the hospitals was a very expensive one and he, along with others,suggested that the goods might be obtained more cheaply by opening the contract to competition. That was done and a great saving had been effected while the quality of the food was quite as good. Councillor Clegg referred to improvements which, at his instigation, had been carried out in the ward, particularly in the mutters of street paving and lighting. Over threequarters of a mile of streets and passages had been paved or scheduled to be paved in the near future, the cost being £3,091. He had done his best to inclitiae the authorities to reduce the price of gas but up to the present he bad not succeeded. Ha was fully convinced that too much of the ratepayers' money was being spent to push private ends. tie did not intend to enlarge upon that hut possibly he would• say something about it on a future occasion; but money -was being spent to serve private ends that the Council should not spend. He was in favour of a constructive policy. He was disgusted with the many commotions and disgraceful scenes that they had in the Town Council. (Applause.) They were a disgrace to any community. If the men who created the disturbances would turn their attention to a con- structive policy the rates might he reduced consider- ably. He urged the ratepayers to send men to the Council—the .Mayor asked for them—who did not go there to quarrel but to conduct the town's business in a businesslike way. (Applause;) Alderman Treetox said the selection which the elec.ors of Howley Ward male last November in return- ing Councillor Clegg did them infinite credit, because they had in him a man who was scrupulously fair and honest and one who was determined that he would do nothing that was not in the best interests of the ward and of the town. If they rallied round Mr. Pickavance and returned him he (Alderman Tinnion) was sure that he would ably second the efforts of Councillor Clegg in many things affecting the welfate and comfort of the ratepayers. Alderman Tinnion pointed out that although -Mr. Pickavance had not taken part in public work, he had done a great deal to help forward deserving causes, and had worked with a thorough genuineness that denoted the man of the right stamp. lie had done much on behalf of such institu- tions as the Lifeboat Fund and the Infirmary. ! (Aoplause.) He was admirably fitted to show his use- fulness in a larger sphere, and if they returned him they would have is representative of whom they could be proud. He (Alderman Tinnion) sometimes thought the . services of some of the members of the Council were ' not recognized in the way they should be. .Some people

thought Councillors should have more kicks than half- pence, and they generally got them. (Laughter.) He I was therefore gratified at the hearty reception accorded ; to him that night, as it showed that what he had done I had been approved of, and that his services had not been In vain. (Applause). Mr. E. PICKAVANCE,WhO was enthusiastically received I said the Mayor had asked them why they did not send better men into the council. In Howley Ward they had, now their chance (Laughter and applause). He was a , fairly large ratepayer in the ward—he paid about £6O I in rates—and had property in that and other wards. He therefore had some interest at stake and would go in -for economy. (Applause). He was not going to promise anything except that if he were returned he would act in the best interests of the ward and of Warrington. He did not believe in promis- ing everyone £lO,OOO a year and free drinks. (Laughter.) They wanted in the Council independent men who would carefully weigh every matter brought before them and act according to their respective judgments. Tie rates at present were very high. He would not object to 10s. in the £ if he thought the rate- payers got value for their money but he did not think they were getting value. He believed Vi7arrington could be ruled satisfactorily on considerably less that is. Bd. in the £—in fact he did not think the rates ought to exceed Gs. With regard to the paving of streets, he could speak from experience as a cyclist. It had been his privilege to wander through mauy towns but he had never dropped across a worse-paved town than Warrington. Knutsford road, Wilderspool-road,andWinwick-roa.d,were postively unfit for any self-respecting cyclist to ride along. (Applause.) With regard to Warrington Bridge, it was a death trap and should certainly be improved. (Applause.) Warrington should also be much better lighted. Whether it was the fewness of the lamps or the poorness of the gas that was responsible be did not know, but their was something radically wrong. Then main, gas ought to be cheaper to the consumer. If they could get good gas in Widnes at Is. 6d. per 1,003 why should they have to pay nearly 3s. in NVarrington when we had one of the best equipped works in the country ? He also failed to see why electric light should be charged for at the rate of 6d. per unit to small consumers when they got it for .Id. in other towns. Another requirement in Warrington was better housing for the working classes. In the neighbourhood of Back Ship-yard, Bank-street and various passages there were houses which were positively not fit for pigs to live in. For the working classes there should be good, big houses with plenty of sanita- tion and every house with a rental of over ss. a week should have a bath. (Applause.) There was a big plot of land in the Ward set apart for recreative purposes but at present it was simply used as a dumping ground for anything that people liked to throw on it. The ground should be properly laid out like the open soaces ia the Orford, Sankey Bridges and Latchfor-.) districts. A Beautiful Warrington Society had been founded and he wished it every success in its efforts. He hoped that in every wide street in the town, including Church-street, they would go in for tree planting on a large scale and if elected that was one of the improvements he would urge. He had been approached by certain individuals as to his views on the question of a fair wage for Cor- poration workmen. He was certainly in favour of giving a man a fair day's pay for a fair day's work and he honestly believed it was an insult to any able-bodied man to offer him 18s. a week. (Applause.) He did not say what the maximum should be, but he would pay a man whathe was worth. He objected to the missrahle, paltry sum they did offer at times to some workingmen. He did not want to;appear too Socialistic but he know of members of the Council who passed increases of salary to highly paid officials to the extent of £lOO a year with- out protest, but when it came to a question of advanc- ing a:workingman ls.a week they discussed it for a week. lithe electors honoured him with their confidence he thought they would have no cause to regret having done so. (Applause.) Mr. J.km ES LOCKER moved a resolution of confidence in Mr. Pickavance.

Mr. S. WRIGHT, J.P. seconded. He remarked that Mr. Chantler raised a flar,' not long ago and his Con- servative friends fought him but now he said he had dropped that flag because it was not popular. He (Mr. Wright) thought the flag under which Mr. Ch antler was now fighting wes no more popular than the one he h..d lowered. (Applause.) Mr. SHERBURN supported and said the particular interest Mr. Pickavaace's opponent sought to represent in the Council was fully represented at present—infect he (the speaker) thought a little over-fully either directly or indirectly. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. PICKA.VANCE ansnered several questions put by members of the audience. He was not, he said, in , favour of municipal dwelling houses because they had not worked out very successfully in other places. He was, however, in favour of a municipal lodging house. .` Are you in favour of reducing the charge for the first class plunge bath to 4d. ?" was another question. Mr. PICKANANCE replied that he was. If they could reduce it to nothing he would be better pleased. Another question was "Are you in favour of a minimum wage of 245. per week for able-bodied Cor- poration workmen ?" , Mr. PICKAVANCE said he was practicaltly in favour of that. One thing was certain and that was that he should always go in for paying a man a proper day's wage for a proper day's work. He would not, however, pay an able-bodied man 245. a week if he was only worth 12s. and scamped his work. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman passed on the motion of Mr. James Critchley.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By " Ovallst."l

The air is full of talk of the decadenco of English Rugby football, the prowess of the New Zealanders, and the suggested rappr,chvnent between the Rugby Union and the Northern Union. Of the decadence of the English club play, I don't think there is much doubt, the international matches of recent years have proved that England is the lagging nation, while the wholesale slaughter at the bands of the Antipodean players have revealed the nakedness of the land as governed by the E,R.U. There is, without question, better and keener football under the Northern Union, and so far as the international contests are concerned I a fifteen chosen from the Northern Union would pro- bably uphold the honour of the old country in the way it should be. But even this does not say 1 that we can equal the performances of the New Zea- landers. A. prominent member of the Warrington club, in whose judgment I have the fullest confidence, says the visitors are the finest team he has ever seen, I and under average conditions he des not know where and by whom they are to be beaten They play the Rugby game as no team in these isles plays it, and their displays are 3 revelation. There would be no fear of Association supplanting Rugby, says my informant, if all clubs adopted the methods of the , visitors.

A writer in the "Morning Leader" deplores the sham amateurism and the want of real enthusiam for the game in the E.R.U. which have rendered the English teams such easy prey to the Colonials. He says :—" To one who has a real enthusiasm for the game, and believes it to be as superior to Soccer as billiards are to marbles, it is a grief to see the way in which a one-sided amateurism allows a visiting fifteen to be thoroughly trained, and refuses to allow a home team to be prepared at the same coat similarly provided."

I don't know whether the disappoin+ment at Northern Unionists being debarred from trying their strength with the New Zealanders has had anything to do with it. but within the past week we have had suggestions from both Hull and Barrow that an attempt be made by tll3 Northern Union to patch up the feud with the E.R.U. Personally, I should be very glad to sea Rugbyites once more united but I cannot imagine any possibility of such a fusion coming to pass yet awhile. If the E.R.U. would relax its iron- bound severity and admit the professional, as is done in all other games, then the difficulty might easily be overcome. There is no reason why ainitonrs and pro- fessionals should not mix oa the Rugby field,when they are allied at asswiation, golf, cricket, and every other sport which has attained magnitude and popularity. Bat we know the E.R.U. ! It pre- fers to cling tenaciously to its sham amateurism and Ices the international trophy year after year, rather than be honest to itself and the world at large. Northern Unionists will only be asking fr a snub, in my opinion, if they suggest re-entering the E.R.U. , fold as professionals. However, even a snub can do no harm, and may possibly result in sowing the seed which will bring Rugby football into line with other games for which Englishmen stand unrivalled.

New Zealand's match with Yorkshire has been allocated to the Headingley (N.U.) ground at Leeds. where a 30,000 crowd should be ensured. The match Nvill take place on Wednesday December 13, four days after the Cheshire match at Birkenhead Park. Local enthusiasts will, therefore, have two fair . _
chances of seeing the all-conquering Colon'als.

Warfngton did not do anything doughty enough on Saturday to merit first place in these notes this week. Vet they were not disgraced at Oldham. Considering the weak team which- did duty, a defeat by 8 points to nil was nothing to cavil at. And there was not even that mach diffecence between the teams. Warrington's defence was excellent, while forward and half-back they quite held their own. The weakness was in attacking power—pace on the wings being sadly lack- ing. Here Oldham had the advantage, hut nowhere else. They gave a display which does not speak very well for their resources, and the game was of decidedly poor quality. I am afraid that a Rugby Unionist or New Zealander, witneising this battle of League champions and Cap-holders, would not have been much impressed by the prowess of the Northern Unionists. And yet what better match could have been selected by such a critic for the purposes of a co.nparison

On the Warrington side, chief praise for pu: ting up such a determined struggle, must go to the forwards, and to Hockenhall, Isherwood, and Knight among the backs. These three were always doing something of an affective nature, and the support of some of the men now on the casualty list would have turned defeat into victory. Fletcher again played a strong and resource- ful game for the winners, and was welt backed up by Tyson and White. The others were like the Warrington reserves, mediocre. Just a final word about Hewitt. His debut was by no means unpromising. Lack of speed is his chief disqualification for first-class football. As a tackler and fielder he is excellent, and did good wcrk in this respect at Oldham.
Runcorn still show an unbeaten record, and ,St, Helens provided them with an easy 2 points on. Satur- day. There should be a battle royal a week hence when Warrington are due at Irwell-lane.

Boardman, Thomas, Presto; Jolley, Belton, Swift, Cook and Harmer, forwards. The re-appearance of Hallam and Kenyon should give the side more con- fidence, and I hope both men will find their form at • once.

IThe "A " team, though so depleted by the calls of the seniors on Saturday, managed to score a cteditable win over Oldham "A." in the presence of a fine crowd. They have another stiff engagement to-day at Chadderton, but should pull through alright with the selected dozen, which is C. The Warrington players are turning out to-day with numbers stitched to the backs of their jerseys. This is for purposes of identification, though not by the police !

• Hockey. Birkenhead Park have rather over estimated their strength, and it would have been wiser if they had been content to remain another season among the junior organizations. On Saturday the Stockton Heath Club paid them a visit, and ran up a score of 6 goals to none.

At all points of the game Stockton Heath were the better side, and if they had taken the game seriously, they would have no doubt doubled the score. W. Richardson was again to the fore, obtaining 4 goals out of the six. He has now obtained eleven of the nineteen goals scored by Stockton Heath this season.

—— The second team just managed to win by 2-1, after a hard fight. Stockton Heath had the assistance of H. Smith for the first time this season, and as he showed all his old form, it is to be hoped more will be seen of him. IThe club record up-to-date is : Goals
P. w. L. D. For A'gst Stockton Heath I. Stockton Heath 11.

The second team this year are a good side, and are to be strengthened nest month by the addition of a first- class forward. There is every hope of another good player, who has been tried for his county while out of the town, coming back; and if he does he has promised to throw in his lot with the Stockton Heath club.

This week the club play Oxton, and a good game should be seen. The first team who pity at home should just about win, but tho second, who will lack the assistance of P. B. Ilawtin, may not find success so easy.

div.head: PRIMITIVE fiIETHODIST SALE OF WORK.
div.p: PRIMITIVE fiIETHODIST SALE OF WORK.

During the week the members of the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church have held a successful sale of work, organized with the object of liquidating a debt upon the working of the church. The sale com- menced son Wednesday when there was a large attend- ance at the Opening ceremony. Mr. R. BRIDGE, who presided, said there was one pleasing feature of the sale of work and in connection with the church and schools—the way in which the young people had taken up the work which lay before them. He thought the interest which the young people were taking in the progress of the church showed that they had a great future before them. (Applause). COuncillor Foust-Law said he knew the people of Legh-street were a hard working and a deserving people and ha hoped that, in that effort their labour would be crowned with success. He believed in sales of work as they enabled all to help and prevented the responsibility being thrown on a few shoulders. He hoped the sale would be e success and had pleasure in declaring it open. (Applause). ! Mr. JoHN Gl:uremia explained that up to two or three years ago they were in the ‘Varrington and Widn !circuit. %Then the circuit was divided, they had to take co:er all responsibilities and the income not equal- ling the expenditure they were involved in a debt. They were, however, he was pleased to say on a fair way to solve the difficulty and hoped that in the future sales of work would not be necessary, as they were making material progress. (Applause). lie moved a vote of thanks to Councillor Porshaw, the chairman, and the Rev. John Yonge for their presence. (Applause). The Rev. C. L. STOWE seconded and the vote waft heartily accorded. Mr. JOHN GRIFFITits presided over a large attend- ance and said that in the past they as Christians had neglected their duty with regard to municipal and Parliamentary elections. He believed however that the 'Christian Churches intended making up for what they had lacked in that direction. tie thought the , results of the recent Parliamentary bye-elections showed very forcibly what the trend of public opinion would be at the coming general election. (Applause). I Aar. Ilicaatas said he believed with the Chairman that as Christians they bad a duty as citizens to work 1 for the benefit of the town and should enter into public life in order to keep out those men who would only be a curse. They might not all be able to speak but they could work and vote for righteousness and truth and ; for those measures which went to the uplifting of the ' masses. (Applause.) div.head: Warrington v. Oldham.
div.p: Warrington v. Oldham.

Owing to the misfortunes which have befallen so many players, Warrington were only able to send a weak team to Oldham on Saturday. No less than half-a-dozen regular members or the senior fifteen were absent, while Oldham turned out at full strength. Beautiful weather favoured the fixture and there would be quite 10,000 people on the Watersheddings ground. Teams : Oldham—R. L. Thomas, back ; Carpenter, Fletcher. Maclean and Tyson, three-quarter backs ; White and Cash, half backs ; Ferguson, Vowles.Hatn,Sraith,Avery, Topham, Owens, and Wilkinson, forwards. Warrington—Knight, back; Jordan, Isherwood. Hewitt and Harris, threequarter backs ; Brooks and Hockenhall, half backs ; Boardman, Thomas, Preston, Cook, Belton, Jolley, Harmer and Swift, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Ff. Smith, Widnes; touch judges, Messrs. McGowan, Broughton Rangers, and Lancaster, Rochdale Hornets.
Ferguson set the ball in motinn and Warrington quickly invaded the home half, Preston and Swift being

to the fore with a smart dribble. A lofty punt, how ever, almost brought about Warrington's downfall for Knight misjudged the ball and it was left to Hewitt to pluckily save under the posts. The Warrington forwards again secured the ball and Hockenhall smartly trans- ferred play to centre, where Ferguson tried at goal from a penalty and failed. Cash eluded the Warring- ton halves and kicked up field, but Knight repelled the invasion in fine style. Strong scrummaging and judicious running and punting by Isherwood took play to the home quarter. A nice kick by Hockenhall enabled Brooks to grass Thomas on the line. Cash relieved, but Knight marked coolly and Preston had a shot at goal. The range was fairly long, but the kicker made a fine attempt, the ball just dropping under the cross-bar. Warrington maintained the upper hand until a wild pass by Hewitt gave the Oldham forwards possession. A race down the Meld followed, Knight just beating Ham by a stride and kicking dead. Oldham scrummaged close in and passing by White, Fletcher and Tyson resulted in the latter just getting over at the corner. Half-time. Oldham 1 try, Warrington nil. In the second portion the game was almost confined ta the Warrington half, and time after time it seemed as if the Oldham score must be inlreased. The game grew exciting, and after several displays of roughness the referee administered caution. The Warrington defence was very reliable and tbreequarter time had passed when a luckly flying kick by Cash having found touch a yard from the Wirepullers' line, White got a pass from the scrummage and made an opening for Fletcher to score under the posts. Ferguson improved. Result—Oldham 1 goal, 2 tries (S points), Warrington nil.

LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON "A V. OLDHAM "A."

Played at Warrington on Saturday. Warrington were handicapped by the absence of several regular players, Knight being substituted by C. Ashton, whilst Kenyon found himself unable to turnout, and Forster was trans- ferred from the forwards. In the early stages of the game Warrington had an excellent opportunity when Lloyd intercepted a pass, and transferred to Short. who mulled. The attack was maintained, and after Davis , had made a futile effort to break through, Wills eased the pressure. The relief was only of a temporary nature. Davie,next made a big effort which led up to a tangible record, a passing movement ending in Short scoring at the corner. The kick at goal was a failure. Oldham next had a turn of attacking, and Brierley made a gallant attempt to cross. The locals exhibited a capital defence, and when the teams crossed over the Warringtonians led by one try to nil. Turning round Warrington had to defend, and Oldfield missed a capital opening for the visitors. From a penalty Tetlow placed a goal. War- rington improved in the later stages of the game, and Fairhurst executing a good dribble, the visitors were in difficulties, and Garside scored. This ended the day's scoring, and Warrington thus won by two tries (six points), to Oldham one goal (two points).

LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP. , FIRST ROUND. WALiCF,R'S BREWERY NT. RUNCORN lIJGZFIaL Played on the ground of the former on Saturday before a good attendance. The visitors won the toss, and commenced in earnest, but their stay in the home quarters was short. Bate got possession from the pack, and passing between Berry and McWhirter, resulted in the ball being taken to the quarter flag. Cross kicking gave the locals little advantage, a good defence pre- vailing. For off-side play, the visitors were penalized and Berry kicked a goal from an easy position. Half- time : Walker's Brewery, two points ; Runcorn High- field, nil. The second half had not long been in pro- grass before the locale increased their lead. Berry received the ball, and after beating several opponents, gave to Timmins, who transferred to Cartwright, the outside man scoring. The kick at goal was unsuccessful. The game was again forced to the other end, and Fleming started a passing movement which led up to Berry scorinr, a good try. The same player failed to augment. scoring now until the finish, the game was of an end-to-end nature, but nothing further was scored. Final : Walker's Brewery, eight points ; Runcorn Highfield, nil.

ISTOCKTON HEATH V. LIVERPOOL OLD BOYS "A."— Played at Liverpool on Saturday. Stockton Ileath kicked oft and were early attacking, hut the attack was spoilt by a forward kicking the ball dead when out the I line. From the drop out, the Old Boys attacked a try re- sulting. This was converted. liven play followed for a time but the Old Boys again took up the attack an unconverted try Lei ig scored. Half-time, Liverpool Old Boys eight points, Stockton Heath nil. From the restart Stockton Heath attacked strongly hut again injudicious kicking spoilt their efforts. From a line out the Old Boy's scored again, the goal kick failing. Stockton Heath now attacked J. Daintith scored an unconverted try. Liverpool added a fourth try. Result : Liverpool Old Boys "A " U points, Stockton Heath three points.

div.head: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.
div.p: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.

A jumble sale in connection with the above was held on Saturday, the object being to raise funds for a sewing class in preparation for a forthcoming bazaar in : id of the Yission Extension Scheme Fund. The Rev. J. Manning in explaining the object of the sale referred to the great need for the extension of the premises. He was sure the appeal for help which was being made would be heartily responded to, and that there was a good time in store for those who were labouring so earnestly in that part of the circuit He hoped the sale would be a great success. Mr. J. B. Isaac, in opening the sale, said he was always glad to visit Ellesmere-street He was pleased to see that at last their hopes of a better building were being real- ized, and heartily wished the sale would be successful in helping to carry on the work of extension: -Mr. J. Upson proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Isaac for opening the sale and Mr. J. Ellison seconded.—The chairman and the Rev. W. Mellor were thanked for their presence and support on the motion of Mr. Llewellyn, seconded by Mr. J. Taylor.—The proceeds of the sale amounted to about £l3.

div.head: HOW IT WAS OBSERVED AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: HOW IT WAS OBSERVED AT WARRINGTON.

There was very little in the nature of public cele- bration of the Nelson Centenary at Warrington. In response to the request of the Mayor flags were dis- played by many of the townspeople and some build- ings were pleasingly decorated with shields and portraits of the hero of Trafalgar. On Sanday the preachers at most of the places of worship alluded to the anniversary.
MR. JAMES DODDS AND THE CELEBRATION.

Mr. James Dodds made a fitting reference to the celebration at the first of a series of popular concerts held in Bold-street schools on Saturday evening. He detailed the events of Trafalgar day, pointing out that at 11 o'clock, when the great battle was coming on. Nelson seemed to be labouring under the impression that he would die that day, and he wrote words that ought to be brought before the people of England to show that our great men, though perhaps weak in many things, had some grand points, and were also religious men. At eleven o'clock be wrote these words :—"May the great God whom I worship grant to my country, and for the benefit of Europe in general, a great and glorious victory; and may no misconduct in anyone tarnish it ; and may humanity after victory be the predominant feature in the British fleet. For myself individually, I commit my life to Him who made me, and may His blessing light upon my endeavours for serving my country faithfully. To Him I resign myself and the just cause which is entrusted to me to defend. Amen. Amen. Amen." Before he died, Nelson expressed the hope to a friend that he had not been a very wicked man, and he was known to pray continually. He (Mr. Dodds) thought it w ell to remind , the audience that Nelson was something more than a ' great naval leader, and his conduct should be an incen- tive to them to do their duty. He died at the age of 47—a short life—havinglestablished England's supremacy and crushed the greatest dream of Napoleon. He (Mr. Dodds) had been struck with the fact that 100 years after the year in which Nelson was born there was born a man who was 47 years of age that day,one who, he believed, would make a far greater mark in history than even Nelson. He referred to President I Roosevelt. who was only 23 when he was elected, and opposed the introduction of Imperial party politics into civic work, such introduction in the control of a city like New York, or Warrington, bringing about extravagance and civic corruption. He was beaten. They were all beaten at times, but Roosevelt stuck firm ' to duty, and he had since done more to promote peace than even our own King. In Roosevelt they had a man who, when he died, would stand as high in the estimation of the world, as Nelson did to-day. (Applause).

div.head: LESSONS FROM NELSON AND TRAFALGAR.
div.p: LESSONS FROM NELSON AND TRAFALGAR.
Sermon by the Rev. John Yonge.

Preaching at Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening the !Rev. John Yonge took for his subject " Lessons from , Nelson and Trafalgar." It might possibly,he said,be felt I by some that the celebration of Nelson's victory over the French a century ago was singularly inopportune. We lived to-day in far happier times when England and France were neither enemies nor rivals but as close in friendship as they were in neighbourhood.The two nations were busily cementing mutual cordiality and complete reciprocity of relationship. Did it not therefore seem as if the attempt to revive the national enthusiasm for Nelson and Trafalgar were somewhat perilous, as being likely to create a chill in the happier international relations of to-day. It was, however, reassuring and indicative of the true feeling predominat- ing in British hearts to-day that the Nelson wreath which had gone from the Manchester Navy League to deck the Nelson monument was accompanied by another to the memory sof the French and Spanish sailors who fell in the battle. People were trying to say how deeply they felt that the long enmity between England !end France was an episode that was closed for ever. The further question might arise ;as to whether it was fitting for that celebration 1 to have any place in Christian Churches and pulpits, It I was the commemoration of a victory which created indescribable havoc in the navies of both nations which might have been prevented had the principles of Christian righteousness and peace been supreme in the councils of the nations which called themselves Christian. There might be some who would demur to honour being paid in such a service as that to the memory of a brave and patriotic commander like Nelson whose personal fame had suffered tremendous discount by serious private and personal delinquencies. He was by no means unsympathetic with such feelings as those. There was a good deal to be said in their justification yet upon closer consideration there was, perhaps, even more to be said on the other side. If diligent care be taken to avoid all selfish and anti-Christian glorification I of British pluck and prowess to the detriment and dis- honour of the fine qualities of the nation which was 'their own foe, if the centenary of the event be used I supremely for expressing national gratitude to God for the signal deliverance then wrought from a wasteful enemy who had destroyed the peace of the whole of Europe, and if it be also used for the commemoration of the heroic devotion to duty which Nelson and all his fleet displayed— then surely the results of the commemoration might be ! beneficial in the nation of to-day. If the issue of that battle had been the reverse of what it was, English , history, and the world's history, in the nth century, ; and even to-day, would have been very differently written.li was absolutely impossible Oven to conjecture , what might have been our experience—the greater part of whose life belonged to the century lately closed—or what theirs might be in the life of the present century. If, therefore, ever waehad justification, surely it might he said to has. had it then. It was impossible to ; imagire any other alternative in a controversy with Napoleon. There could be no terms and no compact 1 with that man of daring genius devotio will, unprin- cipled policy, and utterly boundless ambitions. Could he have conquered and subdued the power of this nation not only British power, but British peace, prosperity, •, and liberty would have been terribly set back, if not 1 utterly destroyed. We have, therefore, the profoundest reasons for national gratitude to God for the great victory of October 2lst, 1805. That being the case, it was alike natural and reasonable that they should think with gratitude and honour of the men who wrought that , great deliverance for them. i The preacher briefly sketched Nelson's trials in his early life : how after being sent:to the tropics he was invalided home. He than became despondent but his , despair aroused his resolution and at the age of 18 years he shook off his despondency and exclaimed "I will be a hero and by the help of Providence will face every danger." That was the crisis in his career and he used j to say that in and from that hour he saw an orb of light ' ever going before him, beckoning him to follow. From that day he dated the real beginning of his great ; career. From the hour of that arousal from the lethargy lof despondency his star was ever in the j ascendant and he ever followed its gleam. In 1 that hour Nelson was down as low as any mortal could be found but he illustrated how a strong mind and a resolute will could marvellously compensate for a feeble body. Nelson was not the only lad of 18 who had ! learned the wretchedness of despondency. There might Ibe lads there who had discovered it and felt as if everything were against them. They had reached the ' crisis when either they must sink and faint or swim and escape. Let them take a lesson from the text book of I Nelson that "difficulties were made to overcome" and Iresolve in the same spirit as that shown by Nelson that "by the help of Providence they would face !every danger." From that period in his life Nelsou's progress was remarkably rapid and his career was I characterized by a succession of hair-breadth escapes. 1 It was one of his conspicuous distinctions that he was absolutely ignorant of fear. He never saw fear ; never Ifound out what it was. Possibly had he done so he might have escaped his premature death. His example in that 1 1 was,to a certain extent,worthy of emulation. What young 1 man was there in that audience who would I not he better for a moral courage which dis- dained fear, especially supremely and victoriously , disdaining it. •in the path of duty? Cudoubtedly I there wet-6 paths, conditions and circumstances concerning which every man ought to be filled with a true fear which would keep him away from them. When a man needlessly exposed his body to a peril that , might cost him his life, or his BOW to temptation which would cost him his purity and his honour, surely he displayed senseless bravado and a recklessness which were not virtues but vices. Possibly bad Nelson feared to tread some doubtful and delicately perilous paths wherein he heedlessly ventured, his fame would not have been besmirched with an odium which even to-day deteriorated from the fulness of the honour which his splendid achievements deserved. There were paths of thought and desire which were dark with peril as they mieht cajole the soul into deeds which were deeds of guilt and shame. There was room for wholesome and restaining fear in each man's life. The fear to imagine evil lest we desired it ; and lest driven by the force of desire we presently did it. "The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom : and to desert from evil is understanding." The supreme quality which Nelson bad ever and accurately been regarded as embodying in hiscareer was devotion to dutyat seemed to him(thepreacher)that there were ample evidences for the belief that he was continually—at least in his public life—animated by the highest devotion to what he con- ceived to be his duty. Probably no stronger evidence of his devotedness could he found than that which was given in the way in which his fleet at ,that started to instant and unanimous response to his famous signal " England expects every man to do his duty." That could hardly have been if Nelson's general fame bad bs en out of harmony with his words. His officers and men knew the supreme feature of his personality. It

Five Doctors' Special Treatments Failed!

She ;ays : -" Sydney Herbert, who is now 3i years old, is our only child, and we were naturally proud of him when he was born. He made capital progress for six months, and then eczema developed. We attributed it to his teething, and the doctor was of the same opinion. His head was soon a mass of sores, and his face and arms were dreadful to see. He was a constant source of trouble. The sores irritated him fearfully, and we did not know what it was to have a good night's rest with him. We had no fewer than five doctors to see him, and tried all sorts of medicine and so-called remedies, but none of them did him any good. For nine months he was under treat- ment from an electric hydro. in the Midlands, from which medicine and soap were sent, but they made no impression on the sores. He was

IN A DEPLORABLE CONDITION. His hair would not grow, and I had to snake him little cotton caps to put over his head. Towards the last, he was one mass of sores and humours, and for days together I had to apply linseed poultices to draw away the matter from his head, face, and arms. "He was in this condition when his grandfather read of a child who had been cured of a similar disease by Zarn-Buk, and he investigated the case for himself. div.head: LECTURES ON ENGLISH ESSAYISTS. .---- The Personality of Charles Lamb.
div.p: LECTURES ON ENGLISH ESSAYISTS. .---- The Personality of Charles Lamb.

was far too late inithe day to attempt to deprecate its sterling quality. Had it been other than true its falsehood would have long since been exposed. He had his country's welfare in view through- out his career. In private life, unhappily, he fell into serious moral default but he could ever appeal to his conscience and to his God that he had done his best at all hazards to do his duty to his country. No other man of his or any time loft after legacy to his country- men than Nelson left in his famous signal. None could conjecture how far and wide that thrilling sentence had affected the minds of men. It was to be hoped that its re-presentation in the celebration might stimulate a national revival of the sense of the sovereign obligation of duty. Was not that indeed one phase of moral and religious revival which was most supremely needed ? It was not a call to-day to join the army or to man the fleet England was at peace and had no one to fear. None the less, however, had Britain urgentclaim upon the faithful and even heroic service of its people. A leading London paper bad said" We have a battle to fight and win ; not against the French or Spaniard but against the subtle and evervatino• influences of luxury ; against the habit of grinding the faces of the poor;against corruption and equivocation in high places; against nepotism, favouritism, and public extravagance ' • against land- lordism, liquor and gambling—foes which if permitted free play lead to the decline and fall of even the greatest empire. We repeat England still expects every man to do his duty." He had read also with the heartiest approval the words of a Warringtoniau who in a journal which he courageously edited, said " We shirk our duty obviously and almost wholesale. Our armies are recruited from the slums. Our ships are largely manned by aliens. We cry for war and do our best to dodge the Income tax, and all the time we are devouring all the petty details of the latest cricket match, or howling ourselves hoarse upon the football field, or spending all our evenings and our Saturdays, and often enough our Sundays in knocking everlasting balls around unending golf links. We want to face our national responsibility." Those witnesses were true. There was a crying need for greater seriousness, for a re-action not only in favour of political liberalism but of common sense and moral earnestness. It was to the religious portion of the people that we most look to bring about that much-needed reformation. It was in the power of their churches and congregations to redeem and dignify the life of the nation by the restoration of duty as the 1 ideal of personal endeavour and the ruling principle of life. How well it would be if everyone would ' bring himself and herself to restore duty to the throne of life, not advantage, indulgence, ambition or ease. If our empire was to be made permanent and imperishable it must be by the devotion of the people to their personal and mutual duties. He would venture to appeal to every person present: were they really striving to be faithful In the duties of their lives ? Were they paying faithful heed to the duties of religion ; the duties of their own souls ; the duties which they owed to their God and Saviour ? The last lay at the foundation of their real welfare. Let them rule their whole lives. " Fear God and keep His com- mandments." That included the whole duty of man. Face it with loyalty and resolution and they would win their victory and receive as their reward the Crown of Life. Rev. W. Bracecamp and Duty.

The rev. W.Bracecamp preached to a large congregation at St. Paul's Church, on SundLy evening upon" Lessons from the life of Nelson." He said the church was or should be, a temple of ponce, but he ventured to think that in the victory of Trafalgar they might trace the finger of God, and be was sure that the hero of Trafalgar "being dead, yet speaketh." They would not spend time ; in praising either themselves or their fathers. There ; should be no bonstin,, about their army or navy,uo hero- worship, no blind eulogy even of that great commander ,! who laid down his life for them. But they would praise the God of heaven, who gave Nelson his daring and his strategy, who used that imperfect instrument, and the I feet under his command for the accomplish- ; meat of his own far-reaching purposes. Nelson's voice would be heard as long as England was ! a nation, calling his countrymen to high purposes, and beneficent aims. What a sermon he presched to them that day. How he pleaded with them to do their duty, and what a duty it was they had to perform. They had responsibilities and opportunities of which he never dreamed. More than three millions of men looked to England for justice and protection for their laws and liberties ; over eight millions of square miles were under the British flag. Did they make that word "Duty" the biggest word in their vocalulary ? Did they make I the ruling principle of their lives their duty to God and their duty to their neighbour ? Did they say like Garibaldi : " God first and our country next ?" To do their duty under all circumstances was not an easy thing. It meant hardship, self-denial, running counter to many of their natural feelings and desires. It meant frequently no earthly reward or recompense, no crowd save one of thorns. The only true life was a life of duty, and every life of duty had its cross, and its crown of thorns. What desecration there was to-day of the Sabbath , The mischief to this country by neglect of the duty and privilege of worship was incalculable. The nation which went away from God must go to ruin. Once cut the cross out of England's flag and it ceased to be the glorious emblem of freedom and victory. Once drive religion out of the home, the school, trade and amuse- ments, and they might write : " Ichahod, the glory is departed," over against the name of England. He (Mr. Bracecamp) dare not pass over the one grave blot in Nelson's life' He should think it cowardly and unworthy of the minister of God so to do. They would say, perhaps, that such a fall as his, such a lapse from honour and purity was only too common, and that there was no need to speak of such things. But he answered that sin was no less sin because it was common, and ! moreover,' that he hardly knew of a case so strange, so pitiful as rtis. It was one of the most sad and instruc- tive things in all biography. The lesson his frill taught I was " Let him that thinketh he staudeth take heed lest

he fall." "Consider thyself lest thou also be tempted." The salient lesson of Nelson's life was that to conquer their own evil nature was a harder task and a greater triumph than to take a city or destroy a fleet, but the searcher of hearts, the God of infinite pity, knew how to make allowances.
At the conclusion of the service, Mr. E. Wilkes, who presided at the organ, played" The death of Nelson," and " Rule Britannia," the congregation also singing a verse of" God save the King."

DEIR CHILDREN, I have awarded two prizes this week, one a picture postcard album, to Ida Doney, who has sent me in twenty-four names of new mem- bers for the League, and the other a beautiful box of Fry's chocolates, to Hannah Martin, who Ws the first to send in correct solutions to Puzzles. I have received a great many answers to these puzzles, and nearly all were correct, so you must all try again, and let me have the replies as soon as you possibly can, so that you. may stand a good chance of a prize. lam Publishing two letters this week. They are both very interesting, and you will see that one is sent by an American nephew, now living in England, I shall give a prize to the 'one who sends in the beet storyette next week. Ido not mind whether it is a true story or an invention,, but it must not be more than about twenty-four lines. You can count how many words go to a line by looking at the letters, etc., printed below. I hope- you will all try and get fresh members, and remember you can get a very nice • Prize by sending in twenty-four names. I will not write any more now, so with all good wishes to you from
UNCLE NED.

DEAR UNCLE NED, I hope you wilkaccept me as a member • of "the League." I will be twelve years of age on the 30th of this month. On Wednesday • next our " Babs." will be four months old. She is such a sweet little thing. She was laccinated not long ago, and her arm was ever So bad. I am in a football team, which was defeated yesterday by 2 goals to 1. The match was hardly fair, however, as they had the stronger team by four men. Early in the spring • I use to collect birds' eggs, of which I had • several, including throssell's, blackbird's, and a yellowhammer's. I have not got any pets, but I collect foreign stamps, being the possessor of five hundred odd. My little brother also collects. I am learning to swim, and my mother says that she will get me a season ticket to the baths for next year. My little brother is in Standard 2; I am in the Seventh. It was a Pleasant surprise to me when the Children's Corner was started in the "Examiner." Roping to be successful, I remain, Yours truly, KENNETH WILLS.

MY DEAR UNCLE, I wish I'd been a member of your League from the first; but I guess I couldn't, as I only came away from America this Fall (Fall, you know, is the name we call your autumn season by). Well, I see you want a story or 'yarn from some of us Cornerites. I'm not much of a hand at yarning, but I calculate the following will just fetch 'em. It's how I amused myself during last vacation. Poppa one day brought me home a Bantam Rooster. Well, it just did me to see him strut about and hear him crow. Of course, I had to •. look after him, so it wasn't long before we be- . earns gnat friends. Poppa suggested that L should drive him, so he helped me to make a set ef linen harness, and the cart we made cut Of a cigar-box, with a couple of wheels fixed on ts it; then we put the rooster in, and after a few turns up and down the front of the house, We would come back t-nd I would tie him up near the porch and bait him with a few ".• grains of corn and some water. Perhaps this • feeding was what made him enjoy the fun so Well that he began to crow in harness. Poppa thinks that his vanity was pleased because of •, the sensation he caused. It may have been - that.
Your American Nephew, 0. H.

The men made their guns ready, and gave dmber Tim an extra pistol to put in .his belt,
_ . . so that he might light with all his might and help save their lives. But when they came to look for Captain Duck, next morning, he was gone. He had joined the Indians.

- Then the men at the stage station were very much afraid; for they had been very cruel, not only to the cripple but to all the Indians, and they knew that if they fell into their enemies' hands, they had no right to expect any mercy at all. The next night the Indians set the woods on fire, and all the land was dark with smoke. The great pine-trees were falling across the road, and no soldiers, nor anybody, could come to help the men shut up in the little log fort, and surrounded by the blazing forests. The men looked one another in the face as the air grew dark and dense from. the smoke, and shook their heads sadly—for they believed their time to die had come. About ten o'clock one morning, the Indians appeared behind the stables and began to fire on the fort. They took tpe horses out, mounted them, and then set fire to the stables. And now there was little hope, for the flameo would spread to the fort,' and then all must perish. The smoke was so dark and thick that the men were almost choked. They could not see to shoot the Indians, for it was like night. "What can we do?" cried the men shut up. in the fort, and hiding their eyes from tho smoke. "The Indians will not come .near enough for us to see them and fight. If we go out to find them we shall be shot 'down from behind the rocks and trees, and not one of us will live to tell the tale."
"Let me go out," said little Limber Tim. "If I can find Captain Duck, I will save you all."

They hurried the boy through the great wooden gate of the fort, as he tied a white towel on a ramrod and held it high over his head in the thick smoke. Then the men bolted the great gate and left the brave little fellow to do his best with his white flag. By and by, the boy with the white flag on the ramrOd came pounding at the gate, and the men .gathered around wild and eager as they opened it. "What luck? What hope?" "Well, if you will all leave your guns and go out one at a time down the stage road and never come back here an more, you can go." "Never come back here any more?" cried one man, as he jumped totvard the gate; "catch me comb' back here any more, if I ever, get out of this!" and. he leaped out through that gate like a newly sheared sheep •leaping over the bars. Then another followed and another, all feel- ing very much ashamed of the way they had treattd the boy. But somehow they did not have the manhood to hold up their heads and say so. , When the men had gone, glad to go and never thinking of looking back or ever return- ing to the Modoc country,. Captain Duck came hobbling in. The Indians helped Tim to put out the fire and then went. away, taking all the stage horses and guns and blankets with them. So when the soldiers came, three days after, they found only these two in charge of the fort,—little Limber Tim and Captain Duck. The Government left some soldiers there after that, and Limber Tim was made station-master by the stage company! He was the youngest station-master, I sup- pose, that ever was on the border. When I passed by there, last year, on a visit to my parents inpregon, I saw him once more. But he is a man now. He has long hair, a small, black moustache, and wears two pistols in his belt, for the frontier ways prevail in that country still. As for poor Captain Duck, he is shorter in the legs than ever, I think. His face is deeply wrinkled now, and his long black hair has turned as white as are the shining snows of mighty Mount Shasta when seen against the cold, blue sky above. He never speaks to any one. But he loves Limber Tim with all his heart, and never is long away from his side nor out of his sight if he can help it. Captain Duck was sitting in the chimney- corner by the great log fire, smoking his pipe, when I saw him last. He was looking straight Into the fire—thinking, thinking. And what was he thinking about Maybe he was think- ing about the dead stage driver who had struck him with a.whip. It may be so. It may be so.

" Mother: "I'm sure I don't know; but go and se what baby is crying about, and tell Johnny to stop throwing things at people in the street, and make George and Kate cease fighting, and tell Dick that if he doesn't stop blowing that tin trumpet I'll take it away from him."

"Billy, how did you lose your finger?" "Easily enough," said Bill. "I suppose so, but how?" "I guess you would 'a' lost your own if it bad been where mine was." "That does not answer my question." "Well, if you must know," said Billy, "I had to cut it off, or else steal the trap."
