div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Service of Song.

On Sunday econing the choir of the Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street efficiently rendered the beautiful ervice of song " Little Dot,' which was listened to ad much enjoyed by a large congregation. The solos nd duets were very tastefully rendered by Mrs. Wood, Miss Lee, Miss Hughes, Miss Dutton, and Miss S. Lee. Mr. Jackson was the organist, and Mr. James Proffitt, of Fearnhead, was the reader.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

At theusual meeting of this society, on Sunday, Mr. Beswick, who presided, spoke upon the helpful- ness and inspiration received from the poetry and song of the P.S.A. meetings. Mr. W. Hickman dwelt upon the great question of the unemployed, and gave some of the causes of the very large number of men in this country who were out of work. He said it was pitiable to see large numbers of willing men who were able to work, but who because they had lived over forty, fifty and sixty years, could find nothing to do. In these days we called upon the Government to do something for such people. If more was spent upon the person, the family and the homes, by the great careless and squanderers, and the great drink spenders, we should soon see a happier state of things.—Then, in the moral and spiritual world, there were too many unemployed, too many neglecting their duty. If every moralist and Christian man would do his duty, we should soon see a happier state of things.—Messrs. W. Lowe and G. Smiley also took part iie.the meeting. Mr. A. Griffiths sang " The death of Nelson," which was very much appreciated. Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. The Secretary welcomed three new members.

div.head: Hill CHM.
div.p: Hill CHM.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held in Hill Cliffe , Baptist Chapel on Sunday and Monday:the chapel being ! prettily decorated for the occasion with an abundance of flowers, fruits, tinted leaves,golden corn, and autumn foliage, the gifts of the friends of the chapel. The pulpit and communion had been decorated under tbp superin- • tendence of Mrs. Hughes and Miss Mather. Others who ; helped in the decorations were Mrs. Dodd, Mrs. King, t Mrs. Wheeler,Mrs. Wilde,Mrs. Williams,Miss E. Mather, Misses Moss,Jones,Anslow,Dodd,Morton, Bouchier,Hall, Berry,and Messrs. Joseph Moss,Wheeler and Wilde. There ' was r. fairly good congregation at the service on Sunday • morning. The preacher for the day Mr. J. W. Deakin, delivered a practical discourse. Harvest hymns were ' sung and Mr. James Strange presided at the organ. In j the afternoon the chapel was crowded to overflowing. ; The chief attraction of this service was the visit of the Legh-street Primitive Methodist choir who contributed ' the sacred cantata, "Esther the beautiful Queen," which under the able leadership of Mr. Spruce was rendered IThe different characters and parts were admirably taken by the following : —Sopranos: Esther the Queen, Miss A. Bridge ;Maid of Honour,Miss A.Woodland. Tenors: Mordecai, Mr. J. H. Corrin ; High Priest, Mr. J. I Phillips. Contraltos: Zeresh, Miss L. Fairhurst ; Prophetess, Miss L. Snelling. Basses: Ahasuerus, Ithe King, Mr. E. H. Pearce; Haman, Mr. George Gough. Baritones: Hegai, Mr. Alfred Spruce; Harbonah, Mr. E. IVlairs. Conductor. Mr. A. Spruce; Organist, Mr. Fred Podmore. In ; the evening the chapel was again crowded. Mr. Deakin preached an eloquent sermon on "What is life?" , The choir rendered the anthem " 0 Lord, how manifold are Thy works" under the leadership of Mr. J. M. ! Muir, Miss Jones taking the solo. Mr. Strange and Mr. Muir shared the duties of organist at the evening service. The collections for the day proved to be con- siderably in advance of last year. On Monday night i the annual fruit social was held in the school room,when • there was a large attendance. The refreshments and the entertaining part of the programme were in the hands of MisseJE. Mather, W. Jones, Dodd, Anslow, Morton and Moss. Thanks were accorded to all donors, decorators, and helpers, and a very enjoyable evening was spent. Ths total proceeds (£l3) were in excess of of last year, and larger than any preceding occasion.

div.head: I ST. MARY'S, LATCHFORp. Annual Sermons in Aid of the New
div.p: I ST. MARY'S, LATCHFORp. Annual Sermons in Aid of the New
Church.

By the erection of the handsome new church of St. Mary at Latchford considerable debt has been incurred, and on :the occasion of the annual charity sermons special efforts are put forth with the object of reduc- ing the outstanding balance. The object naturally appeals to adherents of the Roman Catholic Church in Warrington as well as to many friends who are mem- bers of other denominations, and large congregations assembled last Sunday when the charity sermons were preached by the Rev. J. B. Jagger, the well- known Jesuit preacher. In the morning Mass was sung, the Rev. Father D'Arcy being the celebrant. As usual, the choir had devoted special attention to the I music, and Mozart's Ninth Mass was rendered most , expressively. Mr. J. Babbitt interpreted the solo ' passages with feeling. As an offertory piece " 0 Cor Jesu " (Moorat) was given, the soloists being Messrs. Joseph and B. Bate. The voluntary was " Exultet " (Moomt). Mr. Peter Bate ably presided at the organ. Inn powerful sermon, the Rev. J. B. JAG GAR dealt ' with that wonderful mystery of Godliness, as St. Paul called it,—the Incarnation of Jesus Christ. The Incar- nation meant that they had one divine Person ' —the second Person of the Blessed Trinity— subsisting in two natures—the nature of God and the nature of man. What a mystery it was That which was infinite and had no limitation was by the Incarnation united to that which was created and finite. The mystery, continued Father Jaguar, was above his reason-, though it was not against it. The same God who was the Author of his faith was the I Author of his reason, and therefore reason and faith could never contradict each other. Reason could not teach him all things became he was dealing with an infinite Person and his own mind was finite. There must be mysteries and truths which that poor human m lad of his could not fathom. He did not believe in the 1 Incarnation because he could substantiate and prove it ' with his reason.He believed it because Christ had revealed it and had told him that it was so. There was nothing in that against reason. It was lonly that reason could only go so far, that it could not go beyond its own power or advance beyond its own light. But reason had nothing to say against the possibility of such a union as God in His infinite might and power had drought hi the Incarnation. Above all the Incarnation was the manifestation of the love of God. The end of all religion from the very beginning of our race was the one fundamental idea of union with God, and the Incar- . .

nation satisfied that craving. By means of the ' Incarnation we had been made one with the Father I—it was the glorification of God and the , glorification of man, ;Ind should 4 impress us with the dignity of human nature. No one henceforth might I ever slander or treat human nature lightly. It was something for all time most sacred and holy, because it had been knit to infinite holiness. The preacher con- chided by asking his bearers to repay something to Christ for all he had done for them by. helping on the Ncork of that mission.
FATHER JAGUAR REPLIES TO CRITICISMS OF THE ROSARY.

There was again a large congregation at the evening service, when the Rev. Father Jaggar spoke at consider- able length in defence of the Rosary. Against that form o prayer two charges were made—that it was vain repeti- tion and that it was unscriptural. That it was a prayer which involved repetition was self evident but asithe Rosary was a prayer in which they made their petitions and requests in the best possible form it could never be regarded as vain repetition. A child rapidly learnt how to express that which it desired and so whenever it wished to obtain a favour it used the same form of making the request. Could such method a procedure be regarded as vain repetition ? Most certainly it colld not, and therefore he asked where could be the vain repetition in an oft addressed prayer whereby they sought to gain those favours which they desired from Almighty God? The Rosary was not vain repetition and whatever form of prayer they m,ght use, if they found it gave the best expression to their desires. that prayer could never become vain repitition. Father Jaggar proceeded to deal with the contention that the Rosary was anserip- tural. if there was a prayer which was scriptural, it was the Rosary. He pointed out that the prayer was founded upon the Scriptures, and caused them to medi- tate upon the mysteries of the Scriptures. The prayer had many great advantages. It was suitable for the old man on his death-bed, and could be lisped by the youngest child, so simple was it. At the present time We were faced by great evils. One was that men,more than ever, refused to lead lives of self-sacrifice. The Rosary taught them their duty in that respect. Another evil was the gross materialism of the times—the way in which men and women spent their time seeking amuse- ment and diversion. Improvements in the condition of life had made the obtaining of amusement and personal comfort more easy. He was not condemning anything which led to the greater happiness of mankind but there was a great danger of men regarding this world not as a place of pilgrimage but as final. There was a danger, and a very great danger, of them losing sight of the

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. HIGHER CRITIC.—With the reply of '6 Free Critic " last week we think the correspondence on Chinese Labour might cease.—En. "Ex."

div.head: Councillor Peacock and the Labour Party.
div.p: Councillor Peacock and the Labour Party.

Sir,—ln your issue of the 21st instant appeared a report of a speech delivered by Councillor P. Peacook in support of his candidature for Bewsey Ward. He is reported to have said " He had been specially thanked by the Labour Party for hi. services." May t be per- mitted to state that in no way has he been specially thanked by the Independent Labour Party for his services.—Yours sincerely, T. JONES, Secretary I.L.P.

tin the speech we reported Councillor Peacock did not suggest that he had been specially thanked by the I.L,P. By "the Labour party " he meant various members Of that body,who have at different times personally thanked him for his services. In view of the above letter such an explanation is perhaps necessasy in justice both to the I.L.P. and to Councillor Peacock.—En. "EL"] National Service. Sir,—! am as much delighted by your assurance that you put principle before party as .1 am astonished that you put freedom before national defence. Surely this is somewhat illogical for where does your freedom come in if your defences are unsound and your country con- sequently open to invasion? You are alarmed lest universal training should result In our having an Army such as Germany and France possess—lest a moderate period of service shall be extended to one of two or three years. I cannot see that there is much ground for your fears seeing that this is a democratic State and that the decision whether we have any tralning at all rests with the people. One word more. You refer to my avoiding the term "Conscription.' I do so advisedly, because it is a misnomer. it refers specially to that form of compul- sory service where choice is by ballot with power to buy substitutes. Such a system is most unjust and ex-hypothese inefficient. Universal or national training on the other hand makes no monetary or class distinc- tion. " Duke's son, cook's son " it is all the same and herein lies the truly liberal and democratic principle of the National Service League proposals, which should in consequence appeal to all liberal minded men.—l am, etc., GEORGE CROSFIELD. ,

Sir,—Members of the National Service League will heartily agree with the greater part of your leader on " Conscription " contined in your issue of Oct. 14th. You remind us that Lord Esher has said that " the British public would be very unwise to approve of con- scription." This is undoubtedly true. Conscription with odious inequalities, its injustice, and its .special privileges for the rich can never be expected to appeal to the mind of the British citizen. But at the same time the facts confronting us in relation to the question of Army reform are so serious that they call for some measure of a most drastic character. While we believe that reasonable encouragement should be given to the " Volunteer forces," it is obvious that in the face of the report of the Norfolk commis- sion and the emphatic opinions of many high military authorities, including Lord Roberts we cannot afford to continue experimenting along lines of uncertainty, but should at once take up this question as a National one, and as one in connection with which every British subject must consider his own personal responsibility. Reference is also made to a recent speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfleld on the "Army, Navy and Auxiliary forces." Evidently Mr. Crosfield's solution of the problems con- sists in the maintenance of " powerful auxiliary forces for Home Defence." He thinks that these can be secured by giving greater encouragement to the citizens to become volunteers, and suggests a greatly increased expenditure for this purpose. But does not this amount to an actual destruction of the Volunteer system, and the substitution of a mercenary force which would ultimately lead to the extinction of the highest type of patriotism ? Mr. Crosfleld is undoubtedly right in say- ing that " powerful auxiliary forces are 'required for home defence." Those who desire to know how very far from powerful and how utterly inadequate in the face of possible contingencies these forces are at the present time, should read carefully the speech of Lord Roberts, who Mr. Crosfield and Lord Esher also, must admit to be the greatest military authority of the times. What we require is a system for the defence of the citizen by the citizen, by every man in the nation doing ungrudgingly his own fair share and not looking to those of his fellows who 'feel disposed to volunteer, to fight their own battle and his also. Further if, as must be admitted, the discipline and training of the volunteers is beneficial in respect of both physical and mental development, why should not every man in the nation participate in these benefits. lam pleased to note that a phase of this work the importance of which has been frequently emphasized by the National Service League is receiving the ! approval of the school authorities in several of our large towns. I refer to the introduction of military training in the higher grades of our public schools. We have dropped the question of religious education, why not substitute elementary:military drill? And thus while helping. ' to improve the physique of the boys teach them something which may qualify them to defend their home and country if called upon in the days to come. —Yours sincerely, 71, Hood-lane, Warrington.
G. DALE.

Sir,—Will you allow me space for a comment on the leader in your last issue entitled" Universal Train- ing " ? I am glad indeed to see that you say: "The state of our Army and auxiliary forces is far from satisfac- tory and inefficiency is widespread." Anyone indeed who reads even a little of what the best authorities have said and written about the dangerous state of our land forces must be convinced of this. But you go on to describe the proposal of National training as "extreme," "conscription in a mild form," and "neither the sole nor the best means" for solving the problem of National defence.

Firstly, the proposals of the National Service League are so far from extreme that they are the minimum amount of training we could do with, to be really useful at all, and they are expressly put forward to save us from the real and hateful extreme of long. service—

miscalled conscription—which many say wilrhave to be instituted in England for the sake of her safety, unless a milder substitute is adopted. National training such as obtains in Switzerland is not a_ mild form of con-

div.head: K. L. AIARKEL.
div.p: K. L. AIARKEL.

Sir,— In your issue of Saturday last a letter appeared signed "John Morton, Secretary of the Social Service League." If the motives prompting same were as well known to the general public as they are to the members of the League Committee areply would be unnecessary. Permit me to point out that when Mr. Morton states "nor did I as Secretary know anything at all about it" he is guilty of a deliberate attempt to mislead your readers. Not only did Mr. Morton receive a circular along with a note asking him to attend the meeting, but he was actually present at the lecture. I leave it to your readers to form their own opinion as to the veracity of the person I have to deal with. However, in order that the facts of the case may be placed before your readers, I shall esteem it a favour to be permitted to give a full explanation. At a private conference of Social Reformers held in London a short time ago I had the pleasure of meeting Mrs. Cranston. In the course of our conversation she informed me that she was particularly anxious to visit factories where ideal conditions of labour were in operation. I suggested a visit to the local works and undertook to make the necessary arrangements. Owing to the uncertainty of her movements it was impossible to fix upon a date much in advance and twice within the last fortnight the date to visit Warrington had to be altered. Under these circumstances I abandoned the idea of having a lecture, the risks involved in hiring the hall, lantern, printing, S:c., being too great for the I limited resources of the League. It was not until a few days prior to her visit that I was able to make definite I arrangements for the inspection of the works. I had an I interview with Captain Crosfield on the Thursday. I incidentally mentioned that Mrs. Cranston was willing to lecture, with the result that Dr. Markel with his customary generosity placed the assembly room at our disposal. This offer I gladly accepted and immediately I consulted Mr. Osborne, financial secretary of the Lea.zue. Mr. Osborne at once issued a circular announcing the lecture but made no men- tion whatever of the Social Service League. These circulars were sent out to all interested persons including Mr. Morton. In his case a note was enclosed. As .nany members of the committee as we came in con- tact with were made conversant with the situation and without an exception agreed with what had bsen done. Still,we studiously steered clear of stating in any shape or form that the lecture was being held under the auspices of the league. Moreover the expenses incurred through Mrs. Cranston's visit have been paid by Mr. Osborne and myself. When Mr. Morton states that I claimed to be there as president of the league he stoops to a charac- teristic quibble. I said no such thing, and stated that I had suggested that Captain Crosfleld or Dr. Markel should occupy the position of chairman but that as I happened to be president of the Social Service League and intimately connected with the British Institute of Social Service they thought T ought to fill that posi- tion. _ _

I feel sure that this explanation will cpnvince every fair minded person that we simply tried to do our best under the circumstances. But it it comes to a question of right or wrong who authorised Mr-Morton to write such a letter without consulting the committee,? He knows perfectly well that the committee will repudiate both him and his letter at the first opportunity. Your correspondent's sudden emergence from insignificant obscurity has apparently rendered him incapable of properly estimating his own importanoe,—by and by he will find his level.—Yours truly
HERBERT DIMINICO.
(President of the Warrington Social Service League, Founder of the National Social Service League, and associate of the British Institute Social Service).

us who feel the truthiof it,work hard towards what will mean not only the safety of the State, but a measure vastly beneficial for our own national character, which surely, with its languid discontent, self-indulgence and fecklessness, never stood mole in need of a strong ideal and the touch of discipline than now. These are sad words about one's own country;but to anyone who really loves their country, instead of concealing an evil, acknowledges it and asks tor a remedy. A lady who possesses keen observation and intuition has summed us up thus ; "a nation, whose present main characteris- tics seem to be apathy, conceit, and a general pitiable I, shortsightedness." Conceit, I think, is giving way at present to uneasiness. We feel that many things are wrong!: but the uneasiness does not become concrete in any definite action,and,we shall go down as shortsighted and week-willed in the eyes of all future generations if now, despite urgent warnings from soma of our best men, we remain in our old condition of things and refuse to institute a service which would be an enormous national good in all ways. In conclusion, why fear that national training might lead to a military oppression? Why, a citizen army would be the very thing to make of military training an universally-shared duty, and not a caste apart. Herr Hebei, the great Socislist leader of the Germans declares not for a standing Army' but for a people trained in arms. The late Lord Salisbury, who, however we Liberals may differ from him on many 'points, we recog- nise as a wise thinker and patriotic statesman, declared that " The defence of the country was the business of the people themselves," and responsibility, as any experience of life shows, tends to sober down those who if they had to bear no share in it, might thoughtlessly call for war. "I know only too well what war means," said Lord Roberts, and the suffering and missry it entails ; and my sole object in advocating these defen- sive preparations is to save the country from war." That is the aim of all who are working to obtain national service, but those who—mostly from misapprehension— try to hold back:from this legitimate duty of the nation's men, are inviting war, with its frightful losses and horrors upon England or her possessions at no distant period. I write in no spirit of controversy, but because, being alive to the vital necessity for action with regard to our defences, and realizing the enormous good a national training would do to our national tone and character, I feel it one's duty to try and clear away the misconcep- tions which too often prevent men seeing the grand measure national service will be ; and this must be the excuse for the length to which this letter has run.—l am, sir, yours truly, TRLTDA H. CROSFIELD, (Hon. Sec. N. Wales Branch, N.S.L.)

" The Other Woman " by Mrs. L. T. Meade ; the Walter Scott Publishing Co., Ltd., ss. Mrs. L. T. Meade's striking effort in a new path of fiction is entitled" The Other Woman." It is a novel which deals with a very serious moral problem—one in which the author expresses herself from the woman's point of view with no uncertain note. The question is one which arises from time to time when h man contemplating marriage finds himself face to face with the follies and sins of his past life. In this case as related in the story, Lucy Stanhope discovers the skeleton in her husband's cupboard a week after marrying Mark Stanhope, and immediately leaves him. The character of Lucy is admirably pourtrayed, and one cannot help feeling a certain amount of admira- tion for her. She is a womanly woman, but abnormally sensitive and prone to view things in their wrong proportion. We cannot agree with Mrs. Meade's theory, as worked out by Lucy Stanhope, that a woman is justified in breaking her marriage vows to the extent of deserting her husband on learning that there is "another woman" in the past. Because the " other woman" has borne Stanhope a child in earlier years, Lucy conceives mistakenly that she has only a secondary claim to her wedded husband, and forth- with surrenders him to the one who, in her peculiar moral view, has the prior right. One's sympathy is drawn out to the deceived wife, but it is not possible to justify her conduct by the laws of either Cod or man. Mrs. Meade's story is to this extent original and as it ends satisfactorily we have no doubt that it will be read with both pleasure and interest by many lovers of fiction.

" Lone Marie," by W. E. Norris ; "The House of Mirth," by Edith Wharton ,• and " Kipps " by H G. Wells. Macmillan and Ca., Ltd., Os. lii" Lone Marie "we have one of the most enter- taining of light stories. It tells of the exnariences of Marie Ludlow an American girl who differs in almost all particulars from the typical 'la belle Amerieaine. We have one of the latter sort in piquant Gracie Barron, the millionaire's daughter who Is placed under the watchful and experienced eye of Lone Marie." And yet Lone Marie is neither middle- aged nor forbidding. She has experienced the machinations of men with herself as the objective, but has so far remained heart whole,and with eery apparent intention of remaining so. For a while we see her only as a shrewd judge of human nature, possessing mental and moral attributes which compel admiration. She takes only an abstract interest in the somewhat excited state of the matrimonial market consequent on the heiresss's arrival in London, but eventually one man compels her attention and interest. This is Gordon Heneage, the hero of the story, but otherwise nothing more nor less than a well-bred, captivating scamp. Heneage has a code of honour, be it said, but it is elastic and convenient and has not prevented his being expelled from the shelter of the family roof-tree. Its best feature is that it forbids the telling of lies to Lone Marie, for whom the graceless Gordon early conceives a respect. Meanwhile he sues for the hand of the !heiress with Lone Marie's tacit permission until complica- tions ensue. Marie finds him out and herself out at the same time. She puts a spoke in his matrimonial wheel and discovers that she loves him herself. Self- flagellation and effacement follow, and so does Heneage. He boldly pleads his suit, with Marie, but she declines and eventually succumbs to the persistence of an old admirer. The one weak spot of the story is that so 'insusceptible a person as Lone Marie should so soon fall in and out of love with Heneage. Had she married him it would have been a fitter ending. Mr. Norris, however, tells a very clever story in admirable language, and his efforts deserve warm appreciation. " Pannell's Reference Book " ; the Granville Press Ltd. _ _

We have just received from the Granville Press, Ltd., a volume entitled " Pannell's Reference Book," which is intended to, and we are sure will, supply the long-felt need of a complete book of reference in a single handy volume, a book that can be easily and readily consulted on any question arising in ordinary reading or conversation, or for information on every- day topics 3nd subjects of general interest. It will include an English dictionary, a Guide to the English Language, a Medical Guide, a Legal Guide, an Educa- tional Guide, a Commercial Guide, and a Dictionary of General information, tha last-named supplying for all ordinary purposes the place of the many-volumed Encyclopedia. With Pannell's Reference Book at hand on the table or desk,one is fully equipped to meet any query or difficulty that is likely to arise in reading, writingoor conversation. The question will naturally be asked. How can one book be made to include so much? Partly by superior printing and general production, which has allowed of the use of small type, and conse- quently of the introduction of an enormous amount of matter without in any way inconveniencing the reader, but chiefly by the most careful and judicious selec- tion and arrangement of facts. By omitting all minute details and simply giving the broad features of the varioas subjects in clear and concise terms, by avoiding everything of an abstruse or highly technical character' and by excluding all facts and particulars that to the majority of persons are void of interest; space has been found within the limits of a single volume for the adequate treatment of all subjects on which information is likely to be required. It is only necessary to turn over the pages of the various volumes of an ordinary encyclopmdia to see how large a proportion of their contents is quite unnecessary for general purposes. A large percentage of the subjects treated is of so uncommon a character that it is only on very exceptional occasions that they are likely to be referred to, and the treatment of the subjects is far more lengthy and exhaustive than is necessary for ordinary requirements. In an ordinary encyclopedia the subjects are arranged without any connec- tion other than which the alphabet affords. Pannell's Reference Book serves a double purpose as a book of information on this or that particular at short notice, and also as a book largely suited for con- tinuous reading and study. Moreover, Pannell's Reference Book claims to be a book equally suited to the home and the office. Nor have the special needs and interests of women been forgotten. They will find hero information help- ful in nursing the sick, many particulars respect- women's education and opsnings for employment, much interesting matter on the correct mode of speak- ing and writing and hints that will aid them in play- ing their part becomingly in society. The volume consists of 98-1 pages, small crown 4to, excellently printed and bound, and is published at Us. Gd. net.

div.head: HIS SCALP WAS IN DANGER.
div.p: HIS SCALP WAS IN DANGER.

"I remember vividly .a.-;;;:e1;;.'.--;:iinessed years ago in the West," writes Ernest Thompson Seton in the "Windsor,"" when my attention was strongly directed to the significance of the war-bonnet. I was living among a certain tribe of Indians, and one day they were subjected to a petty indignity by a well-meaning ill- advised missionary. Two regiments of United States cavalry were camped near, and so, being within the letter of the law, he also had power to enforce it. But this occurrence was the last of a long series of foolish small attacks on their harmless customs, and it roused the Indians, especially the younger ones, to the point of rebellion. A Grand Council was called. A warrior got up and made a strong, logical appeal to their man- hood—a tremendously stirring speech. He worked them all up, and they were ready to go on the war-path, with him to lead them. I felt that my scalp was in serious danger, for an outburst accrued at hand. But now there arose a big square-jawed man, who had smoked in silence. He made a very short speech. It was full of plain good sense. He told them what he knew about the United States Army—how superior it was to all the Indians tribes put together, how hopeless it was to fight it—and urged them to give up the foolish notion of the war-path. His speech would not com- pare with that of the other. He had neither the Eire nor the words—he had not even'ithe popular sympathy, and yet he quelled the disturbance in his few sentences; and as I looked there dawned upon me the reason for his power. While the gifted orator of the big words had in his hair a single untufted eagle-feather, the other —the man with the square jaw—had eagle-feathers all around his head and trailing down his back and two feet on the ground behind him, and every one of them with a bright-red tuft of horsehair at its top, and I knew then that T was listening to the voice of Plenty-Coups, the most famous chief on the Upper Missouri, and I realised how a few words from the man of deeds will go farther than all ' the stirring speeches of one who has no record of I prowess to back up his threats and fiery denunciations." div.head: EFFECT OF MOCORS ON ROADWAYS.
div.p: THE EFFECT OF MOCORS ON ROADWAYS.

It is possible that the motor-car may do more damage to a gravel road than would at first sight seam possible in the case of a vehicle shod with so soft and elastic a material as inda-rubber (writes" Radiator "in "The King") but it is hardly fair only to take into account its effect on the surface when it is abnormally dry. From observations extending over many years I am convinced that in ordinary wet or damp weather the pneumatic tyro has a solidifying effect on a gravel road, except, perhaps, at very sharp turns, where a fast car is apt to skid, and that it rolls in and smooths down the material loosened by the action of horses' hoofs. Speaking particularly of the Portsmouth Road, I have often noticed that towards the end of tbe week the surface has appeared badly cut about by the ordinary traffic, but that after the usual swarm of cars has passed on a Saturday morninn the famous highway looks as if it had been carefully rolled. It is difficult to believe that any unprejudiced and competent authority will be found to assert that a single motor- car can do as much damage to any road, however poorly constructed, as four iron-typed wheels, assisted by the pounding of four, or perhaps eight, sharp hoofs. THE ORIGINS OF "TESS." There are few modern writers who have lent them- selves so little as Mr. Thomas Hardy, to that embroidery of flattery and expatiation which passes for criticism nowadays. The article which Mr. Clive Holland con- tributes to the November "Pall Mall Magazine" goes further than usual, for he has had the rare privilege of ; the novelist's company in,going over the ground of his famous novels, and the ph'itographs he publishes were approved and discussed by Mr Hardy himself. The following remarks concerning "Tess of the D'Urbervilles" are among the most interesting. Years ago, when "Tess " was publishing, Mr. Hardy received scores of letters entreating him to make a happy end- ing to that wonderful story; but he states that he felt it was impossible. He has also said that the optimistic 1 device of leaving the hero and heroine "living happy ever after" always provoked him to a greater horror by its unreality, than the honest sadness which comes of a logical and therefore inevitable tragedy. He has come into contact with many of the grievous hardships inseparable from the conditions of agricultural life in former days. And tragedies of crippled and futile lives could scarcely fail to leave a deep mark on a poetic, i niagina two, and impressionable nature. "Tess of the D'Urbervilles" contains many characters which were more or less drawn from actual life. That 1 of old John D'Urberville, for instance, was suggested Ito Mr. Hardy's mind by a labourer who boasted of a vault in Bore Regis Church as being full of " skelling- tons "of his family, and this worthy was usually addressed by the parson of the parish as Sir John. It was not difficult for Mr. Hardy to trace the descent of a family who from the state of lords of the village had descended to that of labourers. Indeed, Mr. Hardy traced the unbroken pedigree of Tess's family back to the Conquest, and in harmony with the decayed fortunes ; of her house was wrought out the pitiful downfall of Tess herself. "In a measure," Mr. Hardy said," the story of the D'Urbervilles is the story of the Hardys and of many another ancient Wessex family, who by reason of apathy on their own part, or fraud or injustice on the part of others, became dispossessed of the lands , which had been held by them for centuries. But the ; fortunes of my own family cannot of course be ' closely identified with those of the D'Urbervilles. From this High Stoy, nearly a thousand feet above the sea, the traveller beholds some of the most fertile land in England—a wide expanse of country dotted here' and there with tiny villages or isolated farmsteads. Indeed, except for scuttering tufts of white which I bespoke the presence of conies amid the bracken and 1 the heather, and the faint sound of the larks' notes far I in the sky above us, there were no indications of life to be seen or heard. On a clear day, from this high 1 upland, more especially in the clarity of atmosphere which so often succeeds rain, it is possible to see the silver streak of the English Channel to the south-west and that of the Bristol Channel to the north-west, while far beyond this last can be caught occasional glimpses of the hills of Wales, This wonderful stretch of upland, golden with gorse and purple with heather in early summer and in autumn, is a favourite haunt of Mr. Hardy's ; and one would imagine it almost rivalling in his affections the dourer and severer grandeur of the famous " Egdon " Heath. It was, by the way, along the gradually ascending road shut in by high environing hedges and leafy overhanging trees, that Tess had her second meeting with Alec D'Urberville ; and it was from the eastern spur of the ridge I beheld stretched out the beautiful Blackraoor Vale in which Tess spent the earlier years of her tragic life.

Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons have prepared a souvenir picture, beautifully printed in colours by the famous" Oilette " process, on the lines of the very successful " Souvenir" issued by them some four years back, on the occasion of their Royal Highnesses' visit to Australia. As in the case of the Australian souvenir, his Royal Highness has graciously accepted the dedi- cation of this Indian visit souvenir, which is composed of the two latest portraits of their Royal Highnesses, the design being surmounted by the Star of India, and draped by the Royal Standard and the Union Jack, while a beautiful representation of his Majesty's Ship "Renown," in which the journey of their Royal High- nesses is being made, forms the base of the picture. The size of the picture is 19in. by 13in., and with margin complete, platemarked, Win by 21in. Price Is.

THE " KNIGHT OF THE CAMERA." As every photographer knows, the one great difficulty 'he has to contend with is the obtaining permission to photograph the places,persons,and events that are of the greatest interest. Every photograper in the kingdom must envy Sir Benjamin Stone, M.P., the president of the , National Photographic Records Association, whose work was long since recognised officially, and who has accordingly been given opportunities denied to others. In taking upwards of 20,000 photograps of State cere- monies and Parliamentary and local customs, Sir Benjamin Stone has had very exceptional opportunities for carrying out his great task. The conditions have been perfect—ideal. Busy though his life has been, he has for two score years had leisure to devote to his monumental undertaking. For lon', too, invitations have been borne to him on the four winds from people interested in that undertaking to photograph a quaint custom, a rare curio, or an historic building ; and when he has accepted them he has been an honoured guest everywhere, and all possible assistance has been rendered him in accomplishing his purpose. The result is that the selection now being published is cram full of interest that can only be described as enthralling. Take, for instance, the pic- tures of the Proclaiming of Edward VII. King at St. James's Palace on that memorable morning of January 25th, 1901. Photographers will take interest in the reproduction of these pictures, which are printed in full-page size, and by the best processes known, and under the direct care of Sir Benjamin himself. Messrs. Cassoll and Co. are the publishers and the work is being issued in 7d. parts, the first of which is just to hand.

div.head: MR. W. PETER RYLANDS ON THE GOVERNMENT.
div.p: MR. W. PETER RYLANDS ON THE GOVERNMENT.
A Panegyric on "Statesmanlike Legislation."
PROTECTION "THE FOUNDATION STONE OF CIVILIZATION."

Mr. W. Peter Rylands was the principal speaker at a prize distribution at the Conservative Club last night (Thursday) when he delivered himself of the following remarkable panegyric on the present Government : "There is" slid Mr. Rylands something rather depressing about politics at the present. Ihe Conser- vative party have had a spell of newer lasting for the extraordinary period of nearly 20 years excluding a short interval when the Radicals held office with a weak and ineffective majority. How can it be wondered that the pendulum should appear to swing the other way. It may be difficult to give a logical explanation, but the swing of the pendulum is

A POLITICAL PHENOMENOA - which must be accepted as a governing factor in our political institutions. Looked at from lany other point of view the present apparent trend of public opinion seems to be unaccountable. ilt s human to make mistakes and a Government which could conduct the business of the nation for so long a period without taking a single false step would be extra- ordinary indeed. But looking over their record it seems to me it must be admitted that the Conservative Party have deserved well of their country. Who can I deny that the prestige of Great Britain stands immeasur- ably higher in the eyes of the world to-day than it did in 1886,and who can deny that the efforts of His Majesty the King supported by his present Government have placed the cause of peace upon a firmer foundation than 1 half a century ? In home politics legislation may not have been of an heroic character, and no doubt is less in amount than it would have been but for the grossly unfair and obstructive tactics of the opposi- tion, but the record is a ftne one. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. The measures that have been pa,,qed have answered well, and even the most extreme R .dicals would hesitate to suggest their repeal. The Employers' Liability Act recognizes the principle of charging upon the trade in which they are employed compensation for all injuries received by men in the course of their employment. A measure in the true Liberal spirit, and in its novelty almost deserving to be styled Radical. The Education Act, about which we have heard so much, is a wondorful piece of legisla- tion, and touching, as it does, the religious feelings of the people, had to reconcile opinions and prejudices which are well nigh irreconcilable. Of necessity such an Act must be of the nature of a compromise, but as the result the State has obtained the whole voluntary system of education, a system built up by voluntary effort over a period of about 100 years with little or no encouragement from the Government of the day. This system has been secured by the State, together with the whole of the endowments, property and organization, in return for what ? En return merely for the privilege of allowing in each school an insignificant amount of instruction in the religious beliefs and its founder, instruction which the children need not receive at all should the parents not wish it. It seems to me

IF COMPLAINT IS MADE AT ALL it might well be that the State has made too good a bargain. I have a share in the administration of the Fdneation Act, and I know that the old Managers of " the schools have given up their property, are compelled to keep up the structure of the buildings at their own expense, and have bound themselves hand and foot, while the power of the Education authority over them I is practically absolute. The Licensing Act of 1904 is another instance of Statesmanlike compromise. The difficulty in the way of reducing an excessive number of public houses in any locality arises from the obvious injustice of taking away a licence without any reason. A publican having obtained a license from the State has a right to expect undisturbed possession so long as be behaves himself. His position would be intolerable if he had no security of tenure and licenses were granted and rescinded arbitrarily and without reason. Compensation by the State for disturbance has been proposed, but invariably rejected. The difficulty of reducing the number of licenses was apparently therefore insuperable.

STATESMANLIKE LEGISLATION had therefore to satisfy, on the one hand, those who strongly believe that a publican has a quasi vested interest in his license so long as he conducts it properly, and on the other hand those who, while ansious;to see the number of licenses reduced, would not consent to compensation by the State. The Licensing Act of 1901 fulfilled these conditions in a remarkable degree, and found a solution for an apparently insoluble problem by charging the compensation upon the trade itself, a principle somewhat analagous to the principle of charg- ing compensation for loss by accident to a working man upon the trade in which be is employed. I might dwell upon other instances of legislation, but lam content to rest the claims of the Conservative party to the

GRATITUDH OF THE NATION upon those three Acts of Parliament settling for many years three of the most awkward problems with which Parliament has to deal i.e., complete Compensation for working men for accident, the Education question with its religious difficulty, and the Temperance question. But above all I appeal to the record of the Government in the domain of Foreign Policy, where, by a steady and consistent diplomacy they have changed the undisguised dislike and hostility of France and the United States of America into feelings of sympathy and close friendship, and by an alliance with that great nation of the East have done much to secure the peace of the world.

I wish to add a few words upon that subject which you all know I have at heart, but which up to the present has not formed a part of the present Govern- ment's programme. I refer to the question of Fiscal Policy. The promise of better trade, and the improve- ment in the Board of Trade returns has for the moment checked the movement, and furnished an argument, unsound though it be, to those who uphold our present Fiscal Policy. In the old days Germany and America went hungry for orders until our manufacturers were full now the English manufacturers hive to go hungry until our foreign rivals are full. It surely cannot be denied that such a change is a change for the worse. The promise of better things in England is the result of activity in Normany and in the United States. When trade in those countries falls Al! the old trouble will present itself again, slack business, empty order books, and workingmm in want of employment. I would warn you therefore against regarding the present condition as an argument against change, be thankful for better trade if better trade is really coming, but remember that as surely as night follows the day the old con- ditions will come again, and possibly more acutely than before. After all the question is largely one of names, and the most unfortunate fact for those who, like my- self, advocate a change in our Fiscal Policy, is that the two policies have been styled Protection and Free Trade. There is something in the English character which loves freedom, and

THE PHRASE FREE TRADE has a pleasant sound to our ears, and suggests the freedom underlying all our political institutions. The word Protection on the other hand suggests weakness, and seems incompatible with a nation which has prided itself so long on its splendid isolation. It is for these reasons that these names are so unfortunate, and par- ticularly so because the ideas suggested by them are absolutely untrue and contrary to the facts. Our trade is not free. If our people could obtain all they want without paying for it the system might be termed free, but price is purely relative, and cheap things without means with which to buy them may be far less free than dear things if all have money in plenty. A system of free imports under which our manufactures have to contend with restrictions and bounty fed competition at home, and hostile tariffs abroad, seems to me sense- less, and would be far better described by some such phrase as "Protection for foreign industries," than by the misleading name of Free Trade. And " Protection " what des Protection involve ? Just reflect a moment and you will see that Protection is the foundation stone of civilization. Remove Protection and civilization falls to the ground. A country only exists amongst the nations of the world by its power of protecting itself by force of arms. In domestic policy you have instances of Protection on every side. Right in the teeth of what Scientists tell its is the first law of nature, the survival of the fittest, we protect the feeble in mind and frail in body, we protect the weak against the strong, and poor against 1 the rich, children against cruel parents, property against the thief and dishonest man, by the Factory Acts we protect the workman from accident, and by other Acts of Parliament we protect the careless against his care- lessness, the fool against his folly. Every Act of Parliament in fact protects somebody against something. Why therefore when we find PROTECTION IS THE MAINSPRING OF OUR INSTITUTIONS and indispensable to our well-being should we say that in trade and trade alone it must have no place. Instead therefore of our prejudice being against a policy with the name of Protection, surely, in the light of our experience it is entitled to our sympathy. And what is the Protection suggested, not a senseless imposition of high tariffs upon everything of which we are most in need, but freedom to adopt an intelligent Fiscal Policy constructed to our wants, freedom to put a duty qn such things the importation of which is injurious to our trade and to our working population, duties to counteract the evil effects of bounty fed competition, duties to enable us to foster , and conserve our trade with our Colonies, duties to en- able us to bargain with our foreign rivals and secure fair treatment for our manufactures, but, so long as our Government is as it is now in the hands of the people, never duties which would press hardly on the poor, and never duties which could injure our trade or effect the earning of our workpeople. This is the true policy of fiscal reform, a policy approved of by the majority of the greatest political economists in the world, and the , only argument which, so far as I have seen, has ever been brought against it is that it is too difficult to carry out. Englishmen are not wont to talk of difficul- ties when a great object is to be attained, and to refuse to make the effort for the protection, consolidation,and

furtherance of our trade through want of courage for the attempt, would suggest that the old spirit has indeed decayed. Rather do I believe that Nchile people may at present be confused in the proper understanding of this difficult question by dishonest and misleading arguments of party politicians, a time will come at no distant date when the true meaning of the policy of fiscal reform will be properly understood, and the nation with one voice will insist upon its adoption."

div.head: Claim for Compensation.
div.p: Claim for Compensation.

At the Warrington County Court. on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., Ralph Hedley, collier, Burtonwood, sought to recover damages from the Collins Green Colliery Company, for injuries sustained, which resulted in his partial incapacity. —Mr. Bryan (Wigan) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Peace (Messrs. Peace and Ellis) for the respondents.—Plaintiff's case was that on the 28th .February be was working in the mine when his pick struck a piece of ron and caused a spark to fly into his left eye. -In consequence of the injury 11.. e, had not been able to work since that date. Dr. Fox stated that he examined the plaintiff's eye in August. Plaintiff was suffering from a cataract due, either to natural causes or to injury. Certain things led him to believe that it was due to injury. Mr. Peace said his Honour must be satisfied that the inability to work was a direct result of the injury. Respondent maintained that the cataract was due to natural causes. Dr. Jackson, St. Helens, stated that he examined the plaintiff's eye shortly after the accident. It was inconceivable that the cataract could have been caused by the accident. His Honour gave judgment for the respondent with costs.

IThe quarterly meeting of the Warrington Juvenile • District was held in the Independent Methodist school- room, Brynn, on Saturday. Bro. H. Blacker, D.S.J.T., called the Council to order at 3.30 p.m., supported by the whole of the District officers and also representatives from 13 Branches being present. Three branches were not ,represented, apologies having been received explaining their absence. The minutes of the last meeting having been passed' - as read, the District Secretary, Bro. S. Massey, pre- sented his report and statement for the past quarter which showed from the results that excellent work had been done,eleven tents reporting an increase of members, o four tents same as the previous quarter, and one tent 3 decrease of two. Wycliffe tent headed the list by an increase of 21, followed by Johnaclab tent with: 20 members, the net result being an increase of 61 during the quarter, bringing the numerical strength of the District to 1017 members and a gain in funds of £l5 12s. 3d., making the total funds of the District 371 is. 6d. The Tent representatives' reports ware given and adopted. Satisfaction was felt that the work of training the young and rising generation in principles 7 of temperance sobriety and thrift was being so success- k ful in the Juvenile tents. The committee appointed by g the District at the last quarterly meeting for the pur- pose of preparing and instituting it challenge gavel and block for competition amongst the tents for best increase of members presented a report. Rules for governing the same were submitted,and with some slight ; alterations were adopted by the Council. A discussion of an interesting character arose at this part of the meeting on the best methods to be adopted by the Tents for the extension of the order during the winter months and was taken part in by Brethren R. Pasquill, P. Smith, J. Horne, W. Wright, T. Massey and H. Blacker suggestions made being worthy of emulation.

At 5.30 p.m. an adjournment was made into the Ante room where tea had been prepared by the ladies of Bryan Hope Tent. , After tea, a vote of thanks was proposed by Bro. 4 James Horne to the ladies for the excellent provision sl they had made for entertaining the district. Bro. NV. WRIGHT seconded the vote of thanks and took occasion to remind the members present that it I was very fitting that the present meeting should have MI been held at Brynn for it was just 14 years ago with less , than 100 members and not more than £lO in funds that the District was instituted by Alderman J. Dimond, . P.H.C.11. of Southport. They could look back with i pleasure at the results that had been achieved and rejoice that they had now over 1,000 members and a sub- 1 stantial sum of ..i.:371 as district funds. The vote of thanks was supported by Brethern F. Massey, B. Warburton, W. 13axendale and C. S. Fellow and much appreciated. Mrs. W. Baxendale replied to the vote of thanks on behalf of the ladies, and said that it was always a pleasure for friends at Brynn to do 4 what they could in any possible way that would help in the success and prosperity of the Rechabite Order. personally she had taken a deep interest in the work From the moment the adult and juvenile tents were formed at Bryan some years ago,and it was most gratifY ' to see the Juvenile district in such a prosperous condi- tion. She hoped it would do even better in the future. The next juvenile district meeting will he held either at Eariestown or Wycliffe Tent Warrington.

The even' of the evening was a debate between the Penketh mein hers, and friends from Sankey Bridges, the snbjeo" under discussion being "Which exercises the greater power for good, press or pulpit." The title was soille: what of a misnomer, as by the "Press," was mese: written matter, pertaining to religious work, and 0.. J. Midwood was the gentleman to open" the "Press" as we understand it literally to-day. Nl.' the debate in favour of the claims of the pulPir: he attempting to show that there were prea9her7 long before there were writers, and that in his opinicclis 0 the Press did not egerciso the same power as wor ... spoken direct from the pulpit. Owing to his time limit' having expired, the chairman checked him before al; , pleting his case. Mr. Blythe, of Sankey Bridges, t'" ' premier supporter of the ``Press," differed from 11..• i Midwood in his remark that preaching came befert; writing and instanced the fact of the Commandlneu f , being given at a very remote period as being a sort .0,, , ' of routine to lire up to, and also gave his opinion v/P/ I the Press had far wider reaching influences than Or, , I pulpit. Mr. A. The matter was then thrown open the audience for their opinion, and the following spot% on the subject :—Messrs. His of meetings commenced on Thursday night last. abls were continued until Monday night, when he glia,,o celebrated lecture " Billy Bray." The meetings _est been very well attended, and the clever and efir"sioa addresses of the lecturer,have made orlasting lillPreisii n& on the minds of his listeners, and much good doubt ensue from his visit.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, My first term of office as one of your repreontatives In the Town Council having expired, I have to thank you sincerely for this further proof of your confience. In retnrning me again, " this time unopposed," for a further term of three years. I desire to say that I shall continue to place my services. Irrespective of party, at the disposal of the ratspayers generally. The improve- ments that have been effected during the past few years must be plain to anyone residing in the Ward, anT I hope, with the co-operation of my colleagues, that we may effect more in the immediate future. Yours faithfully, JAS. U. CRAIK. Green Bank, Manchester rd.

MUNICIPAL RUCTIONS, 1805. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE TOWN HALL WARD. LADIP,S AND GENTLEMEN, The term for which you elected me as one of your Representatives in the Council has expired, snd I have been request d toallow myself to be re-nominated, and have consented. lam not the nominee of any private Individual, nor have I any private interests to serve ; Indeed, my entry into the Council has meant a consid- erable loss to me in many ways, owing mainly to my sympathy with those who have BO strenuously opposed any member making anything from his position. I shall continue to act on these lines regardless of all con- sequences. Owing solely to the work of the Non-Trading Members of the Council the rates (apart from the new Bducation Rate) were this year reduced 4id. in the £, and, with Councillor Burton, I anticipate a further reduction next year. The charge for 'gas to consumers is too high consider- ing the profit maae. I voted for a reduction this year, and should do so again. My general views as an old Warringtonian are well- known to you, and, if elected. I shall do my utmost to serve my native town and my fellow-ratepayers' I am. Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant. W. BENSON. Sankey Street, October 96th, 190'5.

TO THE ELECTORS OF BEWSEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, A copy of my address having been sent to each Elector, it is unnecessary to repeat same here, I must, however, state in justice to myself in reply to my opponents, I was the only rept esentati ve who moved the rejection of all the increases of salaric: last March to the higher officials and I have been personally thanked by prominent members of the Labour party for my services on behalf of the workingmen. I therefore appeal with confidence to the workingmen of Bewsey to be true to themselves by supporting my candidature on Wednesday next. Faithfully Yours PETER PEACOCK. 135, Bewsey 'Road.

pOUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON MUNICIIPAL ELECTION. NOVEMBER ler., 1905. TO THE ELECTORS OF HOWLEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN. Having been requested bv the Liberal Ward Com- mittee and a Lwge number of independent Ratepayers to allow myself to be nominated for a seat on the Town Council to represent Howley Ward, I have, after serious consideration, decided to place my services at. your dis- posal. Having been In business in the Ward for over a quarter of a century, and taken an active interest in all matters affecting the welfare of the Ward. I think I can claim some small knowledge of your requirements. I may say that I am both a large ratepayer and property owner in the Ward,so that I have some interest at stake, Unlike some aEpirants to Municipal honours, I do not intend to make any rash andfoollsh promises ; but, if elected, you can rely upon me doing my utmost to forward the best interests of the Ratepayers. I a:n in favour of Lower Rates, Better Paved and Lighted Streets and Passages, Cheaper Gas, and Better Houses for the Working Classes. I am strongly in favour of providing a Recreation Ground for the Children of the Ward. and would also like to see the wider streets planted with trees, so as to make the Ward rather more attractive than it has hitherto been In conclusion, I can assure you. if honoured with your confidence, that my best efforts will be devoted to secure the strictest possible economy in our Municipal Expendi- ture coupled with Efficiency and Progress. I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, EDWARD PIOKAVANCE, 67, Bridge street, Warrington.

UNICIPAL ELECTION, 1303.—T0 THE ELECTORS OF HOWLEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— At the request of a large nuniber of ratepa),ers both Liberals and Conservatives in fact all shades of opinion and also having been honoured by the invitation of the Conservative Ward Committee, I respectfully offer my- e-If as a Candidate at the forthcoming Election. I have not resid, d amongst you all these years With- out noticing the requirements of the Ward. and although much has been do ain the way of paving und sanita- tion there is still good work to be accomplished such as an enclosed ground for children which woulA be con- sidered a boon, and might be granted as recompense for the placing in our midst of an Intercepting Depot. Tire present system of making huge profits on th. Gas Department does not recommend itself to my ideas because under it the gas cow unaers derive no direct benefit. We are told that the pronto are given to tbe reduction of the rates, but it is poor consolation to con- sumers to know that they are supporting other depart- ments. I wish you to remember that I am not fighting this Election on personal grbunds. All that I desire is pure and honest government, and so far as lies in my power, I will strive to obtain it. We all have our political views but I would never press them on the Council to the detriment cal the Town's interest. On all matters affecting the welfare of the Working Classes I am deeply concerned. I believe in a living wage for Workingmen and In giving them something to live for, and ty doing this we should be raising their standard of life and comfort. In coarchasion I hope to have the pleasure of calling upon as many electors as possible before the polling day, aryl if the ratepayers of the Ward will only remember that I am fighting for their best interest., lam confident of the decision. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant. THOMAS CHAETLER. .S 2 Mersey Street, Warrington.

COUNTY BOROUGH OF WaURINOTON. MUNICIP aL BLEU lONS, NOVE ABER ter, 1905. iTO THE ELECTORS OF TOWN hALL WARD. LADIER AND GENTLEMEN,— Having been selected by the Liberal Party and at the request of a large body of Ratepayers of this, Ward, I - have. after careful consideration, consented to allow myself to be nominated as a candidate to Represent you on the Town Council. I consider your Representative should bs just, without tear or favour, and willing to serve only the interest of th,i ratepayers. I wou d support the stresnthening of the Bye-laws so that all streets and passages should be made before any house is tenanted. I would support more open spaces in all the wards, or the use of day school yards, as playgrounds. I am also in favour of Municipal Bowling Greens. I would support the Fair Wage Clause in all contracts, and a living wsge to workmen under the Corporation. I would support the reduction of the price of gas, believing that the large profits made tram same should benefit the consumers. These and all measures having for their object the ' Improvement ci the Town, would have my hearty support. If you do me the honour of electing me as your ! representative, it shall be my constant endeavour to warrant your c mfidence. lam, ladies and gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JAMES CIIITCHLEY„ ! 6, Bold it., Warrington.

The radiation was found to affect a photo- graphic plate after passing through twelve thicknesses of aluminium foil, each 0•C031 milli- metre thick; but on the addition of a thirteenth layer all photographic action ceased, and the ionising power of the rays also disappeared. The , remanent velocity of the rays ss as, however, t'i'l 60 per cent. of its original value. STRENGTH OF SAND. Over fihirty years ago M. Beaudernoud, a French savant, proved by experiment that a quantity of dry sand, placed in a box of thin sheet iron, or even in a canvas bag, and sub- jected to a slight compression, forms a mars capable of resisting a pressure of sixty tons, with- out breaking or even straining the box or bag. The sand, however, romains perfc-ftly divisible. so that if a small hole be made in the box or bag it will flow slowly, and with so little force that a small piece of paper pasted over the opening will check the flow, even with the sixty tons' weight upon it.

"The Mikado." • ' The clo'sing performance of " The Mikado" attracted a crowded audience to the Parr Hall on Saturday evening. The opera went with a delightful swing and encores were frequent and hearty. At the close, the "three little maids " were presented with beautiful fans, and also received bouquets or boxes of chocolates, while the Mikado was the recipient of a box of cigars. The popular opera secretary, Mr. Newcombe, was presented with a handsome case of pipes in recognition of his efforts to promote the com- fort of the performers, while another prominent figure of the opera received a" reminder" in the shape of a Japanese doll. h.S.P.C.C. Bazaar. A grand bazaar was opened on Tuesday in the Town Hall, Chester, in aid of the funds of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. The inauguration of this effort to liquidate the debt, or at least a portion of the tight, which the society has been justified in incurring, gave every indication that it would fulfil the hopes of the pro- moters. The Marchioness of Cholmondley performed the opening ceremony in the presence of a large gather-i, ing. Tbe various stalls were most artistically , arranged, and at the Warrington anti District Stall there was a host of fancy articles, which were sold by Mrs. F. Aylmer Frost, Miss Massey, and Mrs. W. An unique entertainment is this week being pre- sented in the Parr Hall, in the shape of a pictorial ; representation of our Eastern ally—Japan. Panoramic views of the leading cities and the principal places of I note in the land of the Mikado are shown and I interesting information is given respecting each view. The programme is rendered more attractive by a brief variety ,entertainment the vocal con, 1 tributers to which are Mr. Arthur Rowntree (tenor ' Miss Bessie Hardman, Miss Nita Smith and Mr. Mark Mills. Miss Marie Tempest, than whom there is no more charming actress on the stage to-dap, is presented by Charles Frohman in " The Freedom of Suzanne," the greatest success of the London season. Miss Tempest's career in the musical world and her magnificent representation in " The Marriage of Kitty" have been succeeded by a marvellous perform- ance as Suzanne. Be fine acting and expression dangerous ground is skimmed over and Miss Tempest has undoubtedly put the seal to her fame as the finest comedy actress we have. Hall, to a dinner at the Academy, as a mark of appreciation of their services, not only; on behalf of the society, but also for the well-being of the town of Warrington. An excellent repast was served. Mr. L. Greening presided over the subsequent proceedings The toast of The society " was submitted by Mr. Madeley,and responded to by Mr.J.Moore )lurray, while that of " Kindred societies ' was proposed by Air.
